Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verse 1:

﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] before Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

The opening with the address "O you who have believed" serves to draw attention to the importance of what follows this address, so that their ears may await it with eagerness.

Their description as ﴿those who have believed﴾ functions as a title for them, along with what its origin indicates of their fitness to receive this prohibition with compliance.

It has already been mentioned, in the discussion of the purposes of the surah, that al-Fakhr [al-Razi] noted that Allah guided the believers to noble character traits, which are either toward Allah, toward His Messenger ﷺ, toward the wicked, toward the present believer, or toward the absent believer. These are five categories. Allah therefore mentioned in this surah five times ﴿O you who have believed﴾, and each time He guided to a noble trait corresponding to one of the five categories, etc. Thus this first address encompasses the obligation of proper conduct toward Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, which heedlessness neglects.

The literal meaning of al-taqaddum (تَقَدُّم, "going forward") is walking ahead of others. Its bare verb is qadama (قَدَمَ), from the pattern of nasara, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿He will lead his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Hud: 98]. The intensive form qaddama (قَدَّمَ) by its rule should be transitive to two objects, but that is not attested; rather it is transitive to the second object by the preposition (عَلى, "upon").

It is also said: qaddama in the sense of taqaddama, as if he made himself go forward; so it is intensive but has become intransitive. Thus the meaning of "do not put forward" (لا تُقَدِّمُوا) is "do not go forward."

Accordingly, the verb in "do not put forward" is the present form of qaddama used intransitively in the sense of taqaddama over others, and this verb has no object. From it is derived muqaddimat al-jaysh (مُقَدِّمَةُ الجَيْشِ, "the vanguard of the army"), for the group that goes ahead of it, and it is the opposite of the sāqa (السّاقَة, "the rearguard"). From it is also named muqaddimat al-kitab (مُقَدِّمَةُ الكِتابِ, "the introduction of the book"), the portion that comes before the book. The pattern fa'ala often comes in the sense of tafa'ala, like wajjaha in the sense of tawajjaha and bayyana in the sense of tabayyana; among their proverbs: "The dawn has made itself clear to the one with two eyes" (بَيَّنَ الصُّبْحُ لِذِي عَيْنَيْنِ).

The expression is an analogy, likening the state of one who does an act without permission from Allah and His Messenger ﷺ to the state of one who goes ahead of his companion while walking and leaves him behind. The point of resemblance is being alone apart from him on the path.

The prohibition here is for warning, since no one had yet acted presumptuously against the Law. From this it is inferred that the forbidden advancing is that which occurs when there is the possibility of waiting and the ability to await what the Messenger ﷺ decides by Allah's command, and this indicates that finalizing a matter in the Messenger's ﷺ absence is not blameworthy.

This verse supports the statement of the jurists that the mukallaf (مُكَلَّف, "legally responsible person") does not proceed to an act until he knows Allah's ruling concerning it. al-Ghazali counted knowledge of the ruling on what the mukallaf is about to do among the sciences that are an individual obligation (fard 'ala al-a'yan) for those who face it.

The intended meaning of the verse is the prohibition of finalizing anything without the permission of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Therefore the name of Allah was mentioned before it, to draw attention to the fact that Allah's intention is known only through the Messenger ﷺ.

From His saying "do not put forward" etc., the meaning "follow Allah and His Messenger" is obtained.

The occasion of revelation of this verse is what al-Bukhari related in his Sahih, in the account of the delegation of Banu Tamim, with his chain to Ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "A group of riders from Banu Tamim came to the Prophet ﷺ. Abu Bakr said: 'Appoint al-Qa'qa' ibn Ma'bad ibn Zurara over them.' 'Umar said: 'Rather, appoint al-Aqra' ibn Habis.' Abu Bakr said: 'You only intended to oppose me,' or 'to contradict me.' 'Umar said: 'I did not intend to oppose you,' or 'to contradict you.' They argued until their voices rose over this, and then it was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] before Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak loudly to him as you speak loudly to one another, lest your deeds become worthless while you do not perceive.﴾" [al-Hujurat: 1-2].

Thus this verse is a preparation for the prohibition of raising voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, speaking loudly to him, and calling him from behind the chambers.

It is related from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, that it was revealed because of "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sending a detachment, and the Banu 'Amir killed the men of the detachment except three men who escaped; they met two men from Banu Sulaym and asked them about their lineage, and the two claimed affiliation with Banu 'Amir, thinking that this claim would save them from an evil they feared, because Banu 'Amir were stronger than Banu Sulaym. So they killed the three men and seized their belongings, then came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and informed him. He said: 'Evil is what you have done. They were from Banu Sulaym, and the spoils are what I clothed them with'" — meaning he recognized that when he saw the spoils, and informed them that he had clothed them with it, and that clothing was a sign of Islam so that the Muslims would not attack them; so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ made peace with them. And ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] forward﴾ was revealed, the verse. That is: do not act on anything of your own accord in disposing of the affairs of the community except after you have consulted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. According to this narration, the incident occurred shortly before the incident of Banu Tamim, so their two verses were linked in revelation.

There are other narrations about its occasion of revelation which do not fit its placement with the verses connected to it. Whatever the occasion of its revelation, it is general in prohibiting all forms of the intended advancing.

This verse was placed at the beginning of the surah, preceding the rebuke of the delegation of Banu Tamim when they called the Prophet ﷺ from behind the chambers, because what came from Banu Tamim was of the category of raising the voice in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, and because the dispute of Abu Bakr and 'Umar and the raising of their voices occurred in the matter of Banu Tamim. So this verse was a preparation for His saying ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2], etc., because whoever Allah has favored with this distinction, namely making the finalizing of an action without his command like finalizing it without the command of Allah, is deserving of reverence and veneration, so that one should lower the voice in his presence.

He placed this before the rebuke of those who called the Prophet ﷺ because this is more deserving of attention, since it is the discipline of one who is more deserving of refinement.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿tuqaddimu﴾ with a damma on the taa' and a kasra on the dal, doubled. Ya'qub read it with a fatha on both, on the basis that its origin is "la tataqaddamu."

Al-Fakhr [al-Razi] said, in discussing His saying ﴿O you who have believed, if a wicked person brings you news, verify it﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6] in this surah: this surah contains guidance of the believers to noble character traits, which are either with Allah, with His Messenger ﷺ, or with other members of mankind, and these are of two kinds, for they are either upon the way of the believers in obedience, or they depart from it by wickedness; and one who enters into their way is either present with them or absent from them. So Allah mentioned in this surah five times ﴿O you who have believed﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6], and after each time guided to a noble trait from one of the five categories. He said first: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put [yourselves] before Allah and His Messenger﴾, which includes obedience to Allah the Exalted; and He mentioned the Messenger with Him to indicate that obedience to Allah is known only through the word of the Messenger, so this is obedience to the Messenger following obedience to Allah.

He said second: ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2], to explain the courtesy toward the Prophet ﷺ himself in the matter of good conduct.

He said third: ﴿O you who have believed, if a wicked person brings you news﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6], etc., to draw attention to the way the believers deal with one who is known to have departed from their way, which is the way of guarding against him, because his action is corruption within their community; and he followed it with the verse ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9].

He said fourth: ﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], to the end of His saying ﴿it is they who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], so He forbade what commonly involves disregard of the verbal dealings for which little weight is given.

He said fifth: ﴿O you who have believed, avoid much of suspicion﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12], to the end of His saying ﴿Accepting of repentance, Merciful﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12]. End of quotation.

He means: Allah mentioned an example from each category of noble traits according to what the occasions in this surah required, after beginning with what the surah was revealed for at the outset, so that each example would indicate the rest of its kind and guide to the ruling on its like without burden or tedium.

The Qur'an, in establishing the most important good conduct, took the way of prohibiting its opposites of bad conduct, because averting harm is given precedence in rational consideration over securing benefit.

The conjunction of ﴿and fear Allah﴾ completes the prohibition of advancing before the Messenger ﷺ, to indicate that refraining from finalizing a matter without the Messenger's ﷺ permission is part of the fear of Allah alone; that is, its opposite is not from piety.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ is in the position of a reason for the prohibition of advancing before Allah and His Messenger, and for the command to fear Allah.

al-Sami' (السَّمِيع, "the Hearing") is the One who knows what is heard, and al-'Alim (العَلِيم, "the Knowing") is more general. He mentioned them between the two attributes as a metaphorical warning against opposition, and in that is an emphasis on the prohibition and the command.

[Page 219 continues]

Repeating the call "O you who believe" a second time serves to give emphasis to this matter and to signal that it deserves specific attention, so that it does not become submerged within the first matter. This is among the etiquettes of the believers' conduct toward the Prophet (ﷺ). What is required is observing courtesy in what is more emphatic among dealings, by way of implication (*dalalat al-fahwa*, the reasoning from a stronger case to a lesser one).

This is also a preparation for His saying ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not understand﴾ [al-Hujurat: 4], and it is a lesson delivered to them on the occasion of one aspect of the story of the delegation of Banu Tamim.

The word *raf'* (raising) is used metaphorically (*musta'ar*) for raising the voice loudly beyond the customary level of speech. The raising of the voice is likened to the raising of the body in that it reaches the ears more forcefully, just as raising the body makes it more visible to the eyes. This is by way of implicit metaphor (*isti'ara makniyya*). Alternatively, the delivery of speech with a strong loud voice is likened to delivering it from an elevated place, such as a minaret, by way of explicit metaphor (*isti'ara tab'iyya*).

[Page 220]

The phrase ﴿above the voice of the Prophet﴾ is a *tarshih* (an elaboration that supports the metaphor) of the metaphor in *la tarfa'u* (do not raise), and "above" here is also figurative.

The position of the phrase ﴿above the voice of the Prophet﴾ is that of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to *aswatakum* (your voices), meaning: exceeding the voice of the Prophet (ﷺ), that is, exceeding the customary level in loudness of voices, since the Prophet (ﷺ) speaks at a customary volume.

This adverbial expression carries no restrictive implication (*mafhum*), because it comes in the manner of what is usual. The intended meaning is not that when the Prophet (ﷺ) raises his voice, you should raise yours to the same degree.

The meaning is: do not raise your voices in his assembly and in his presence when some of you speak to others, as occurred in the case that gave rise to the revelation.

From this prohibition there arises the sense of a command to lower voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since the intention is not that they be entirely silent in his presence.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn al-Zubayr said: "After this verse, 'Umar would never speak to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) without asking him to repeat, in a questioning tone." Ibn al-Zubayr did not narrate this from his father, meaning Abu Bakr. However, al-Hakim and 'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Hurayra that Abu Bakr said, after the revelation of this verse: "By He who revealed the Book to you, O Messenger of Allah, I will not speak to you except as one speaks to a close friend in confidence, until I meet Allah."

In Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibn Abi Mulayka said: "The two good men nearly perished: Abu Bakr and 'Umar raised their voices in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

This prohibition is restricted to occasions other than those in which loud voice is commanded, such as the call to prayer (*adhan*) and the takbir on the day of Eid, and other than what the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically permitted, as when he said to al-'Abbas, when the Muslims were routed on the day of Hunayn: "Call out, O companions of the acacia tree." Al-'Abbas had a loud voice.

[Page 221]

His saying ﴿And do not speak loudly to him in speech as you speak loudly to one another﴾ prohibits another kind of loudness, namely raising the voice when addressing the Messenger (ﷺ). This is because the requirement of distinction (*taghayur*) between what is demanded by His saying ﴿do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ and what is demanded by ﴿do not speak loudly to him in speech﴾ must be observed.

The *lam* in *lahu* (to him) is for transitivity of *tajharu* (speak loudly), because *tajharu* here carries the sense of *taqulu* (say). The *lam* thus indicates that this loudness relates to addressing him. The comparison in His saying ﴿as you speak loudly to one another﴾ adds further clarity.

This prohibition includes the conduct of those who called out to the Prophet (ﷺ) from behind the chambers. It thus serves as a transition (*takhallus*) from the introduction to the intended purpose, and the excellence of the placement of His following saying becomes evident: ﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not understand﴾ [al-Hujurat: 4].

The phrase ﴿lest your deeds become void﴾ (*an tahbata a'malukum*) occupies the position of an accusative (*mahall nasb*) after the removal of the preposition (*naz' al-khafid*), the preposition being the *lam* of causation (*lam al-ta'lil*). This is a causal explanation of the thing prohibited, not of the prohibition itself. That is, speaking loudly to him leads you, if you do not refrain from it, to the voiding of your deeds. The voiding of deeds through this is something to be feared, so it has been made the object of the *lam* of causation, turned away from its apparent sense. The implied meaning is: "out of fear that your deeds become void." This is how the grammarians of Basra estimate it in this and similar cases. The Kufan grammarians, however, take it as containing an implied negative particle *la*, so the meaning becomes "lest your deeds not become void," which makes it a causal explanation of the prohibition in its outward sense.

*Habt* (voiding) is a figurative depiction (*tamthil*) of the failure to benefit from good deeds because of what befalls them of disbelief. It is derived from the expression *habitat al-ibil*, used when camels eat fresh green herbage, so that their bellies swell, they fall ill, and sometimes they die. In a hadith: "Indeed, among what the spring produces are things that kill by bloating or cause sickness." His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become void﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5] was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Ma'idah.

The apparent meaning of the verse is a warning against the voiding of all deeds, because the plural with a possessive pronoun is among the forms of generality. The voiding of all deeds occurs only in the case of disbelief, since faith is among the deeds. The meaning of the verse, then, is that failing to guard against bad manners toward the Prophet (ﷺ), after this prohibition, may lead its doer to a great sin that falls upon a great portion of his good deeds, or may lead him to disbelief. Ibn 'Atiyya said: that is, it becomes a cause of estrangement in your souls, so that your beliefs keep slipping backward until that results in disbelief, and thus the voiding of deeds. I say: because failing to refrain from bad manners toward the Messenger (ﷺ) accustoms the soul to persisting in them, so it keeps increasing in them, and reverence for the Messenger (ﷺ) diminishes in the soul, and it moves from one bad thing to a worse, until it reaches the point of not caring about observing courtesy toward him, and that is disbelief. This is the meaning of ﴿while you are unaware﴾.

[Page 222]

Because one who moves from a bad thing to a worse does not perceive that he is gradually taking more of the evil, by virtue of habituation to a thing little by little, until sins overwhelm him, and perhaps the last of them is disbelief, when the soul has become so accustomed to proceeding that way.

It is also possible that what is meant is the voiding of some of the deeds, the phrase being general in form but intended in a specific sense. The meaning then is the occurrence of a reduction in their deeds, by the preponderance of the gravity of the sin of speaking loudly to him. This is unspecified, and none knows the extent of the voiding except Allah, the Exalted.

So in His saying ﴿while you are unaware﴾ there is a warning to exercise increased caution against these destructive things, so that the practice does not become a habit that leads to what voids deeds. Unawareness does not apply to the act of performing the forbidden thing itself, for if it did, its doer would not be accountable, since holding a heedless person to account is impossible.

[Page 223]

Ibn 'Abbas reported: "When the words of Allah the Exalted were revealed, ﴿Do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2], Abu Bakr would not speak to the Messenger of Allah except like one who speaks in a whisper (*akhi al-sirar*), that is, one who speaks privately, quietly. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who lower their voices in the presence of the Messenger of Allah...﴾ the verse."

This sentence is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*), which answers an implied question, since the warning in His words ﴿lest your deeds be nullified﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2], and so on, arouses in the listener's mind the question of what the opposite condition of the one who raises his voice is.

Opening the statement with the emphatic particle (*inna*) serves to draw attention to its content, namely the praise of these people and the reward for their deeds. The sentence also gives the reason for the two prohibitions, by mentioning the reward for the opposite of what is forbidden. This concern is further emphasized by the demonstrative noun in His words ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has tested for piety﴾, together with what the demonstrative carries of an alert to the fact that those indicated are deserving of the predicate mentioned after it, because of the attribute mentioned before the demonstrative.

Since you have already learned that the sum of the meaning of His words ﴿Do not raise your voices﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2] and His words ﴿nor speak loudly to him﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2] is the command to lower the voice in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, the reason becomes clear for turning away from attaching the praise here to not raising the voice and not speaking loudly in the presence of the Messenger ﷺ, and instead attaching it to lowering the voice in his presence.

*Al-ghadd* (lowering) in its literal sense is the lowering of the eye, that is, not staring at a person. Here it is used metaphorically for lowering the voice and inclining it toward speaking quietly.

*Al-imtihan* means testing and trial. It is a form of *ifti'al* from *mahana*, meaning he tested him. The *ifti'al* form here carries the sense of intensification, as in the expression *idtarrahu ila kadha* (he compelled him to such-and-such).

The *lam* in His words *li-l-taqwa* ("for piety") is the *lam* of cause. The sense is: He tested their hearts for the sake of piety, that is, so that piety would be in them, so that they would be pious. It is said: "So-and-so was tested for such-and-such a thing," just as it is said: "He was tried for a thing" and "He was trained for taking up a matter," meaning he is equal to it and not weak in it.

Thus it is permissible to take *imtihan* as a metonymy (*kinaya*) for the firm establishment of piety in their hearts and their steadfastness upon it, to the extent that they are never found in any state other than being pious. This is an allusive metonymy (*kinaya talwihiyya*), because the transition from it to what follows is by way of necessary implication. It is also permissible to take the verb *imtahana* as a sent metonymy (*majaz mursal*) for knowledge, that is, the knowledge of Allah that they are pious. In that case, the *lam* in His words *li-l-taqwa* is connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from *qulub* ("hearts"), meaning "being for piety." Then the *lam* is the *lam* of specification (*ikhtisas*).

The clause ﴿for them is forgiveness﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, and it is the intended element of this resumptive clause. What lies between them is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) to draw attention to its importance.

In the *Kashshaf*, al-Zamakhshari made the predicate of *inna* the demonstrative noun together with its predicate, and made the clause ﴿for them﴾ a resumptive clause. Each has its justification, so consult it.

He (al-Zamakhshari) also said: "This verse, in the arrangement in which it is ordered, places those who lower their voices as the subject of the emphatic *inna*, and makes its predicate a clause consisting of a subject and predicate, both definite. The subject is the demonstrative noun. The resumption of the clause that contains the reward for their deeds, and the mention of the reward in an indefinite form with its matter left ambiguous, both indicate the utmost approval and satisfaction with what those who honored the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did, and inform of the magnitude of the might of the Messenger of Allah and the extent of the honor of his station." End of quotation.

This promise and praise include Abu Bakr and Umar at the beginning, since both of them used to speak to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ like one speaking in a whisper.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verses 4–5:

﴿Indeed, those who call out to you from behind the chambers, most of them do not understand.﴾ ﴿And if they had been patient until you come out to them, it would have been better for them. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This sentence explains the sentence ﴿And do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet, nor speak aloud to him as you speak aloud to one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2], explaining it by example, and this example is the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul).

This is the beginning of the purpose (al-gharad), and what arose from it is what necessitated the revelation of the opening of the surah, so it was opened with it. This is because the warning and the promise that were made for its sake are suitable to be an introduction to the intended subject. Thus there resulted an wondrous composition (nazm badi') and sublime conciseness (ijaz jalil), even though the order of its mention differs from the order of its occurrence in reality. This order also coincided with the matter of the (ordering of) the core, since their calling out from behind the chambers was a form of raising the voice to the Messenger ﷺ, like the raising of voices of some of them over others. So the prohibition against raising one's voice to him was a preface to the mention of their calling out from behind the chambers.

By ﴿those who call out to the Prophet ﷺ from behind the chambers﴾ is meant a group of the delegation of Banu Tamim, who came to Madinah in the year nine, which is the Year of Delegations (sanat al-wufud), and they were seventy men or more.

The reason for this delegation's coming to the Prophet ﷺ was that the Banu al-'Anbar among them had taken up arms against Khuza'ah. It was also said that they had prevented their brethren, the Banu Ka'b ibn al-'Anbar ibn 'Amr ibn Tamim, from paying the zakat. The Banu Ka'b had embraced Islam earlier, but I have not found the time of their Islam. The apparent view is that they embraced Islam in the Year of Delegations. "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Bishr ibn Sufyan as a collector to receive the charities of the Banu Ka'b, but the Banu al-'Anbar prevented them. The Prophet ﷺ then sent 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn with fifty men from the Arabs, among whom there was no Ansari or Muhajiri, and eleven men, eleven women and thirty children were taken captive from them. Then a group of their chiefs came in pursuit of them to ransom them, and they came to Madinah."

Their orator was 'Utarid ibn Hajib ibn Zurarah, and among them were their leaders: al-Zibriqan ibn Badr, 'Amr ibn al-Ahtam, and al-Aqra' ibn Habis, and with them 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn al-Fazari al-Ghatafani. These last two had embraced Islam earlier and had fought alongside the Prophet ﷺ at the conquest (ghazwat al-Fath). Then the delegation came with them. When the delegation entered the mosque, and it was the time of the midday rest (al-qa'ilah) while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asleep in his chamber, they all called out from behind the chambers: "O Muhammad, come out to us," three times, "for our praise is an adornment, and our blame is a disgrace; we are the most noble of the Arabs." In this action they followed the manner of the delegations of the Arabs to the kings and chiefs: they would come to the house of the king or chief and go around it, calling out that they be given permission, as is recorded in the story of al-Nabighah's coming to al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani.

Their saying "our praise is an adornment" was a method by which they would solicit the great for gifts, so the idafah of "our praise" and "our blame" to the pronoun is an idafah of the verbal noun to its agent.

When the Messenger of Allah came out to them, they said: "We have come to boast to you, so permit our poet and our orator," until the end of the story.

Their saying "to boast to you" (nufakhiruka) follows the custom of the Arab delegations of mentioning their glories and their days, and the one to whom the delegation comes mentioning his own glories. This is the meaning of the form of mufa'alah in their saying "nufakhiruka." Most of them had remained disbelievers at that time, and they only embraced Islam after they had boasted and recited poetry to one another.

Thus by ﴿those who call out to you﴾ is meant the men of this delegation. The attribution of the act of calling to the pronoun of ﴿those who﴾ is because all of them called out, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said. However, it occurs in the hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that the one who called out was al-Aqra' ibn Habis. In that case, the attribution of the verb "yunadunaka" to the pronoun of the group is a metaphorical attribution in the intellectual sense (majaz 'aqli), attributing the act of the leader to his followers, since al-Aqra' ibn Habis was the head of the delegation, as one says: "The Banu so-and-so killed so-and-so," whereas only one of them killed him. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72].

The negation of intellect from them is intended to mean the intellect of the courtesy required in dealing with the Prophet ﷺ, or the intellect of courtesy that is absent from their custom which they had practised in the Jahiliyyah, of harshness, roughness and arrogance. There is no prohibition in it, nor does any sin follow from it.

Allah the Exalted said ﴿most of them do not understand﴾ because among them were those who did not call out to the Prophet ﷺ in the manner of their calling, and perhaps the intended meaning is the exception of those two who had embraced Islam earlier.

So this verse is a discipline for them and a removal of them from the blameworthy traits of the people of Jahiliyyah.

Al-waraʾ: behind, and it is a relative direction according to the position of what it is attached to.

The meaning: the chambers are a barrier between them and the Prophet ﷺ, so they do not see him, and so he expressed the direction of one who does not see as "behind" (waraʾ).

And (min) is for the beginning (ibtida'), i.e., "they call out to you with a call issuing from behind the chambers." So the callers, with respect to the Prophet ﷺ, were behind his chambers. One who says "so-and-so called me from behind the house" does not mean behind the doorway of the house, nor behind its back, but some direction of it; and the people calling out were in the mosque, so they were facing the prophetic chambers. Had he said "so-and-so called me behind the house" without the particle (min), it would have been possible that both the caller and the one called were in a direction behind the house, and the prepositional phrase would be a stative complement (zarf mustaqarr) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) of the agent or the object. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

Page 228
﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and then become regretful for what you have done.﴾
This is a third address with which another theme begins, namely the manners of the communities of believers toward one another. The reports have been consistent among the exegetes, from Umm Salamah, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Harith ibn Dirar al-Khuza'i, that this verse was revealed concerning a particular incident. That is because the Prophet ﷺ sent al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'ayt to the Banu al-Mustaliq of Khuza'ah to collect their sadaqat (charity). When news of his coming reached them, or when they were slow in his arrival, they went out to meet him, or they went out to deliver their sadaqat themselves, and they were armed. And it reached al-Walid that they had gone out to him in that state, which is a state not customary in receiving the collectors, and his own soul suggested to him that they intended to kill him, or when he saw them approaching in that manner, according to the variation of the reports, he feared that they had intended to kill him, since there was enmity between him and them from the time of the Jahiliyyah. So he turned back toward Madinah.
(This is what has come in four reports that agree on the description of their going out to him, while differing in explaining what motivated them to that going out, and in whether al-Walid was informed of their going out to him, or saw them, or his soul sensed fear. And al-Walid came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "The Banu al-Mustaliq wanted to kill me, and they refused to pay the zakah." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ became angry and resolved to send Khalid ibn al-Walid to them to examine their affair. In another report, he sent Khalid and commanded him not to attack them until he had verified their affair. And when Khalid reached the abode of the people, he sent a spy of his to observe their condition, and he informed him that they were establishing the adhan and the prayer. So he informed them of what had reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning them, collected their zakah, and returned.)
In another report, they supposed from al-Walid's return that he would suspect them of withholding the sadaqat, so they came to the Prophet ﷺ before Khalid went out to them, disavowing withholding the zakah and the intention of assaulting al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah. And in another report, when they reached Madinah they found the army going out to fight them.
This is the summary of these reports, and they are with chains of narration of which none is in the Sahih.
It has been related that the occasion of revelation of this verse was two other incidents, and this is more well known.
Now let us occupy ourselves with explaining the connection of the placement of this verse after the preceding one, for the transition from it to this requires a link between them. The two incidents are similar, since the delegation of the Banu Tamim, concerning whom the previous verse was revealed, came apologizing for their rejection of the envoy of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who came to collect the sadaqat of the Banu Ka'b ibn al-'Anbar of Tamim, as has previously been mentioned, and the Banu al-Mustaliq disavowed that they withhold the zakah. However, this is contradicted by the great distance between the two times, unless there is an error in specifying the year of the delegation of the Banu Tamim.

Page 229
The repetition of the address with ﴿O you who have believed﴾ and its separation without a conjunction serves to give this theme special attention, as you have learned in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2].
So the sentence is a fresh beginning (istina' ibtida'i) for the connection previously mentioned.
This verse has no bearing on legislation regarding the affair of the Banu al-Mustaliq with al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah, because that was an incident that has passed and been settled.
Al-fasiq (the deviator): one characterized by fisq (transgression), which is committing what the Shari'ah forbids of the major sins.
It has been explained here as the liar, as said by Ibn Zayd, Muqatil, and Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah.
In the condition the particle (in) has been chosen, whose original use is for a conditional of uncertain occurrence, to alert that the matter of the condition's verb is that it rarely occurs, and that Muslims do not undertake it.
Know that the verse does not imply describing al-Walid as a deviator, either explicitly or allusively.
The exegetes have agreed that al-Walid supposed that, as in al-Isabah from Ibn 'Abd al-Barr, and there is nothing in the reports that requires that he deliberately lied. Al-Fakhr said: "Applying the term fasiq to al-Walid is a far-fetched matter, because he imagined and supposed and erred, and one who errs is not called a fasiq."
I say: Had al-Walid been a fasiq, the Prophet ﷺ would not have left off rebuking him and calling him to repentance, for it is reported that he did not add to his saying to him: "Deliberation is from Allah and haste is from Shaytan," since al-Walid's hastening to return was haste. The going out of the people to confront al-Walid in that form was indeed the cause of his suspicion,

since it was not the known custom for tribes to go out to receive collectors. And I reckon that their action was a stratagem by their elders to turn al-Walid away from entering their quarter, out of concern, in the eyes of their common folk, that an enemy of theirs should enter their abodes and take charge of collecting their sadaqat, so that their enemies would reproach them for that, and their lowly folk would be aggrieved. For this reason they took their sadaqat themselves, according to one report, or came apologizing before Khalid ibn al-Walid came to them, according to another report.
This is supported by what came in some reports of this story: that al-Walid was informed of the people's going out to him and heard of it, so perhaps that information was conveyed to him deliberately so that he would fear and return.
The biographers of al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah agreed that he was brave, generous, and of good character and manliness.
Know that the majority of Ahl al-Sunnah hold the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ to be upright (udul), and that everyone who saw the Prophet ﷺ and believed in him is among his Companions. Some added the condition that he narrate from him or accompany him, and al-Mazari inclined to this. He said in his Amali in the principles of fiqh: "We do not mean by the Companions of the Prophet everyone who saw him or visited him briefly; we mean his Companions who accompanied him, supported him, aided him, and followed the light that was sent down with him, and those are the successful ones whom Allah testified to have success." End of quote.
These reports were only seized upon by those who held grudges against 'Uthman, since among their baseless grievances was that he appointed al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah as governor of Kufah. So they applied the verse to other than its intended sense and attached to al-Walid the description of fasiq, and far be it from him, in order that his governorship be invalid. And even granting that the verse is an indication of a specific deviator, why is it not understood as referring to the one who informed al-Walid that the people had gone out to him in order to prevent him from reaching their abodes, intending to make him turn back?
In some reports, Khalid reached the abode of the Banu al-Mustaliq. In some, the Banu al-Mustaliq came to Madinah apologizing. The reports agree that between the Banu al-Mustaliq and al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah there was enmity from the time of the Jahiliyyah.
In one report they apologized for being armed, intending to honor their guest. In al-Sirah al-Halabiyyah, they said: "We feared that he would initiate against us the enmity that was between us." This verse is a foundation for testimony and narration, regarding the obligation to investigate the inner state of one whose piety is unknown. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "No one is to be taken captive in Islam except by upright men (al-'udul)." It is also a great principle in

the conduct of rulers and in the dealings of people with one another, regarding not giving ear to everything that is related and reported.
The address ﴿O you who have believed﴾ is intended for the Prophet ﷺ and those with him, and it includes al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah, since he believed the one who informed him that the Banu al-Mustaliq intended harm to him, and it includes whoever comes after from the rulers and commanders of the believers, because the purpose of it is to legislate the verification of one who is not known for truthfulness and uprightness.
The use of the particle (in) in this conditional indicates that it is something that should happen only rarely.
Al-tabyin (clarification): the strength of making clear, and it is transitive to an object in the sense of abana (to make clear), i.e., examine and clarify. The object is omitted, indicated by his saying "a report," i.e., verify what he has brought, and the clarification of each thing is according to its nature.
The command to clarify is a great principle regarding the obligation of verification in judgment, and that the judge should not pursue hearsay and idle talk, nor yield to roaming thoughts of suspicions and illusions.
The meaning of "fa-tabayyanu" is: seek out the truth, i.e., from other than that deviator. So the report of a deviator becomes a call to inquiry and verification, and is fit to be a basis for judgment in no circumstance; and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "No one is to be taken captive in Islam except by upright men."
The report of the deviator is exposed to doubt and fabrication because the deviator's religious restraint is weak within himself, and weakness of restraint emboldens him to treat the forbidden lightly, and what he reports, whether in testimony or report, by which harm results to another or to the public good. His boldness in this is reinforced continually if he does not repent, feel regret for what came from him, and desist from its like.
Association (shirk) is even more emboldening in this, for there is little regard for restraint in the foundations of shirk.
The indefiniteness of "fasiq" and "naba'" (report) in the context of the condition conveys generality over deviators in whatever form of deviance they are characterized, and over reports however they may be, as if it were said: whatever deviator brings you whatever report, pause regarding it and seek to clarify the matter and uncover it.
The Jumhur read "fa-tabayyanu" with ta then ba then ya then nun, from al-tabyin. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read "fa-tabathbatu" with ta, tha, ba, ta, from al-tathabbut. Al-tabyin is seeking clarity, which is the appearance of the matter, and al-tathabbut is seeking firmness and searching for stability, which is truthfulness.

The outcome of the two readings is one, though their meanings differ. And it is reported from the Prophet ﷺ: "Steadfastness is from Allah and haste is from Shaytan."
As for the placement of ﴿lest you harm a people out of ignorance, and then become regretful﴾ etc., it is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, the lam of causation being omitted. It is also permissible that it be accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi).
The thing that is causally linked by the omitted or implied lam is the tathabbut (verification). So the meaning of its being caused by harm, after which regret occurs, is that verification is the response.
Thus the meaning of its being caused by harm, the final result of which is regret, is that harm is a cause that calls for verification as a means of avoiding it. Therefore the meaning of the sentence is on the negation of the occurrence of this harm, because if a cause is fit to establish refraining from an act, it is fit to lead to its opposite, by the mutual entailment of opposites. A parallel to this causal construction was mentioned in His saying: ﴿lest your deeds be nullified﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2] in this surah.
This warning, arising from acceptance of the report of a liar, indicates a warning to whoever has in mind fabricating a report, of what would follow from his false report of harm befalling people. This is by the implication of the address's sense.
Al-jahalah (ignorance) is used in the sense of the opposite of knowledge, and it is used in the sense of the opposite of forbearance, as in their saying: "He was ignorant, like the ignorance of the sword." If it is the first, then the ba' is for accompaniment, and it is a fixed adverbial phrase in the position of a circumstantial state, i.e., "while you are in a state of lacking knowledge of the reality, having believed the lie." The object of "tusibu" in this sense is omitted, indicated by the context before and after, i.e., "lest you harm them with injury." Most usage of isabah is for delivering harm, and in the second usage the ba' is for transitivity, i.e., "lest you harm a people with an act resulting from ignorance, i.e., with an act of severity and injury."
The meaning of "fa-tusbihu" is "fa-tasirur," because some of the sisters of kana are used in the sense of becoming. Al-nadam (regret) is grief over an act that has occurred. What is meant here is religious regret, i.e., regret over becoming entangled in sin through negligence and abandoning the search for the aspects of truth.
This address contained in His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, if a deviator brings you a report, investigate﴾

is directed first to the believers who are informed (bi-fath al-ba', the receivers), each according to the impact upon him, with whatever reports reach him, according to the differing aims of the informants (bi-kasr al-ba', the speakers).

But this address does not leave those who transmit news (al-mukhbirin, reading the *ba'* with a kasra) free from being held to this verification (*tabayyun*) regarding the reports they carry, and from being mindful of the evil consequence in what they fabricate of fabrications. However, this *tabayyun* differs from the other's *tabayyun* and *tathabbut* (careful verification). The first is the recipient's *tathabbut*, by scrutinizing what he receives of narration or what comes to his hearing of speech, while the other is the scrutiny and discernment of the state of the reporter.

Know that four issues of jurisprudence (fiqh) and its foundations (usul al-fiqh) can be derived from this verse:

The first issue: the obligation to investigate the uprightness ('adala) of one whose state is unknown, in accepting testimony (shahada) or narration (riwaya), before the judge and before the transmitters. This is the explicit meaning of the verse, and we have already pointed to it above.

The second issue: that it indicates the acceptance of a single person (al-wahid) whose reliability in his testimony or narration is free from the suspicion of lying, and who is marked by uprightness. This is part of the implicative meaning (*mafhum al-shart*, the understood meaning of a conditional clause) in His saying: ﴿If a degenerate comes to you with news, then verify﴾. It is a principle of usul al-fiqh concerning acting upon the report of a single transmitter (khabar al-wahid).

The third issue: it has been said that the verse indicates that the original state of the unknown person is lack of uprightness, meaning that there is no assumption of his uprightness. Thus it is obligatory to examine the one whose state is unknown, and his testimony and narration are not acted upon until he is investigated and his uprightness is established.

This is the view of the majority of jurists and hadith scholars, and it is the view of Malik. Others have said: the original state of people is uprightness, and this is attributed to Abu Hanifa. Accordingly, one whose inner state is unknown but whose outer state is known (*majhul al-batin*) is accepted by him, and this is expressed as one whose state is concealed (*mastur al-hal*). The presence of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) among them is a known matter that is not reported as news. The intent is therefore to teach the Muslims to follow what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) has legislated for them of rulings, even if these do not accord with their desires.

The clause ﴿Were he to obey you in much of the matter﴾ etc. may be a fresh, independent resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*).

The result of the two considerations regarding the position of the clause is one, and the coherence of the speech under both assessments is unbroken.

Obedience (*ta'a*) is the action of one who is commanded, what he is forbidden from, and what he is advised about; that is, were he to obey you in what you desire.

The word ﴿matter﴾ (*amr*) here means an event and a pressing affair.

The definite article in *al-amr* is the definite article of genus, encompassing all matters. For this reason it is accompanied by the expression ﴿much of﴾ (*kathir min*), meaning: in many occurrences in which you have a desire to obtain something that contravenes what He has legislated.

This is a qualification excluding his obeying them in some matters that are not among the affairs of legislation, as when he obeyed them in the deployment of the army on the day of Badr in a position that they preferred for taking control of the water of Badr.

*'Anat* (hardship, distress) is the disruption of a matter, either in the present or in its outcome.

The imperfect form in His words ﴿Were he to obey you﴾ is used with past reference, because the particle *law* (lo, "were") indicates the conditional suspension of a past matter. The shift to the imperfect form is because the imperfect is suitable for indicating habitual continuity: that is, were he to obey you in a particular case, and were he to obey you whenever you desired something from him or advised him about it, you would be in difficulty. For some of what they request is harmful to others or to the one who desires it himself, since he may love an immediate benefit that returns to him with harm.

The placement of the predicate of *inna* before its subject in His words ﴿that among you is the Messenger of God﴾ serves to emphasize this state of his being among them, and to alert them that their duty is to rejoice in him and to be sincere to him, because his presence among them is a great honour for their community and a benefit for them.

*'Anat* is hardship, that is: it would befall those who strive for the Prophet (ﷺ) to act according to what they desire, namely *'anat*, which is sin, since they would have deceived the Prophet (ﷺ). It would also befall others *'anat* in the sense of hardship, namely what reaches them from the Prophet's (ﷺ) command being applied in a manner that suits the reality and thereby harms the rest of the people. It may also return as harm to the liar who gloats over his desire at times, so the *'anat* of the one who lied to others befalls him at other times.

﴿But God has made faith beloved to you and has adorned it in your hearts, and has made disbelief, grave sin and disobedience hateful to you. Those are the rightly guided. A bounty from God and a favour. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

The qualification (*istidrak*) conveyed by ﴿but﴾ (*lakinna*) arises from His words ﴿Were he to obey you in much of the matter, you would be in difficulty﴾, because it implies that some among you have a desire that the Messenger (ﷺ) obey them in what they wish him to do, in many matters that they seek and consider beneficial for themselves.

The meaning: But God does not command His Messenger except with what contains the good of the outcome, even if it does not coincide with your immediate desires. This is in regard to what God has legislated of rulings. Therefore ﴿faith﴾ here means the rulings of Islam, not belief in the strict sense, for the term *iman* (faith) and the term *islam* (submission) are interchangeable. That is: faith, which is the religion that the Messenger (ﷺ) brought, has been made beloved to you. This is an exhortation to submit to what the Messenger (ﷺ) commands, and it is similar in meaning to His words, ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not truly believe until they make you judge in what they dispute among themselves, then find within themselves no resistance to what you have decided, and submit with full submission﴾ [al-Nisa': 65]. Hence, His making faith beloved to them is an embedding (*idmaj*) and a concision (*ijaz*). The implied sense is: But God has legislated Islam for you and made it beloved to you, that is, He invited you to love it and to be content with it, and you complied.

In His words ﴿and has made disbelief, grave sin and disobedience hateful to you﴾ there is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) that those who do not obey the Messenger (ﷺ) have remnants of disbelief and grave sin in them. God says: ﴿And when they are called to God and His Messenger, that he may judge between them, behold, a party of them turn away﴾ [al-Nur: 48], up to His words: ﴿they are the wrongdoers﴾.

The intent of this is that they should abandon what is not among the rulings of faith; it is thus of the same kind as His words, ﴿Wretched is the name of grave sin after faith﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11], a warning to them against deviating from the clear path of faith and a turning them away from what is among the traits of the people of disbelief.

Thus the statement in His words ﴿has made faith beloved to you﴾ up to His words ﴿and disobedience﴾ is used for arousing and stirring up resolve to observe faith and to dislike disbelief, grave sin and disobedience. That is: if you have loved faith and disliked disbelief, grave sin and disobedience, then do not desire the attainment of what you desire when the religion prevents it and when grave sin and disobedience call toward it. In this there is an indication that rushing to attain what one desires out of caprice, without distinguishing between what pleases God and what does not, is one of the vestiges of the age of ignorance, one of the traces of disbelief, grave sin and disobedience.

The mention of God's name at the beginning of the clause of qualification, rather than the pronoun of the speaker, is because of the awe and dread that the name of majesty (*ism al-jalalah*) conveys.

It also implies the obligation to embrace what He has made beloved to them and to reject what He has made hateful to them.

The two verbs *habbaba* (made beloved) and *karraha* (made hateful) are followed by the preposition *ila* (to), because they are construed as implying the sense of *ballagha* (conveyed), that is: conveyed to you the love of faith and the hatred of disbelief.

The verb *zayyana* (adorned) is not followed by *ila* as the two verbs *habbaba* and *karraha* are, to indicate that when He encouraged them toward faith and made disbelief hateful to them, they complied, so they loved faith and it became adorned in their hearts.

*Tazyin* (adornment) is making something an adornment, that is, beautiful. 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

*They agreed, my beloved and I, with the dawn: "May God clothe that face with adornment."*

The clause ﴿Those are the rightly guided﴾ is a parenthetical (*i'tiradiyya*) clause of praise. The demonstrative ﴿those﴾ refers to the pronoun of the addressees in ﴿to you﴾ twice and in ﴿your hearts﴾; that is, those who loved faith, whose hearts were adorned with it, and who disliked disbelief, grave sin and disobedience, they are the rightly guided, that is, they are those who stand firmly upon the path of truth.

The separative pronoun (*damir al-fasl*) conveys restriction (*qasr*), specifically restriction of individuals (*qasr ifrad*), indicating that among them there is a group who are not rightly guided, namely those who were characterized by grave sin at the time they were so characterized; if they desist from it, they join the rightly guided.

*Fadlan min Allah wa ni'mah* ("A bounty from God and a favour") is in the accusative as an absolute object (*al-maf'ul al-mutlaq*, cognate accusative) specifying the type of the verbs *habbaba, zayyana* and *karraha*, because that making beloved, adorning and making hateful is of the kind of bounty and favour.

The clause ﴿And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) of the clause ﴿And know that among you is the Messenger of God﴾ to its end, an indication that what is mentioned therein is among the effects of God's knowledge and wisdom. The *wa* (and) is parenthetical (*i'tirada*).
