Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verse 9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿If two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them. But if one of them transgresses against the other, then fight the one that transgresses until it returns to the command of Allah. If it returns, then make peace between them justly and act equitably. Indeed, Allah loves those who act equitably.﴾ Since His saying, "lest you harm a people in ignorance" (the verse) came before, it was among the things that fit the notion of harming a people for two groups of the believers to fall into fighting, because among false reports are reports of tale-bearing (namimah) between tribes. Their danger is greater than what occurs between individuals, and verifying them is harder. Verification may not be achieved until the fire of strife has blazed and regret no longer helps.

In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Anas ibn Malik: the verse was revealed concerning an incident in which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by a gathering in which was 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was on a donkey. The donkey urinated, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stopped. 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy said: "Let go of your donkey, for its stench has harmed us." 'Abdullah ibn Rawaha said to him: "By Allah, the urine of his donkey is more fragrant than your musk." They insulted each other and came to blows. Their two peoples, al-Aws and al-Khazraj, came, and they fought with sandals and palm fronds. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to them and made peace between them. Then this verse was revealed. In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Usama ibn Zayd, there is nothing indicating that the verse was revealed concerning that incident.

This is contradicted by the fact that that event occurred at the very beginning of the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ arrival in Madinah, whereas this surah was revealed in the ninth year after the Hijrah. Moreover, Anas ibn Malik did not state with certainty that it was revealed concerning them, for he said: "It reached us that it was revealed concerning them: 'If two groups of the believers fight, then make peace between them.'" Perhaps this verse was attached to this surah a long time after its revelation.

[Page 239]

103 And on the authority of Qatada and al-Suddi: it was revealed concerning a strife between al-Aws and al-Khazraj caused by a dispute between a man and his wife, one of whom was from al-Aws and the other from al-Khazraj. Each one's people supported them, until they pushed against each other, and some of them attacked others with hands, sandals, and sticks. Then the verse was revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ came and made peace between them. This is more apparent than the first report. Thus it is a general ruling that was revealed concerning a specific cause.

"In" (in) is a conditional particle that makes the past tense refer to the future, so it has the force of the present tense. "Two groups" (ta'ifatan) is in the nominative by an implied verb that is explained by His saying "fight" (iqtataluw), for the sake of emphasis on the agent. The verb was moved away from the present tense, even though the present tense is more suitable to a conditional, because when the agent was to be placed before its verb for emphasis on the subject of the predicate, the verb was made past tense, according to the eloquent manner of speech in such cases, where the conditional "in" precedes a noun, as in His saying: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾ [al-Tawbah: 6], and ﴿And if a woman fears ill-treatment or desertion from her husband﴾ [al-Nisa: 128]. Al-Radi said: The verb that comes after the noun that follows "in" should by rule be in the past tense, though it may occasionally be in the present tense by irregularity. The use of the present tense is weak because of the separation between the jussive particle and its governed element.

The pronoun in "fight" (iqtataluw) refers to "two groups" according to meaning, because ta'ifah is a collective noun, and ta'ifah means a group. This was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Let a group of them stand with you﴾ in Surat al-Nisa.

The preferred reading is that the verb "fight" (iqtataluw) is used to mean intending to occur, like His saying: ﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer﴾, and like ﴿Those who divorce their wives by saying they are like their mothers, then retract what they said﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 3], meaning they intend to retract. This is because ordering reconciliation between them is obligatory before fighting begins, when its early signs appear. This is better than waiting for the fighting to occur, so that the calamities can be averted before they happen, in accordance with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if a woman fears ill-treatment or desertion from her husband, there is no blame on them if they make a settlement between themselves﴾ [al-Nisa: 128].

By this, the connection of His saying ﴿But if one of them transgresses against the other﴾ to the phrase "fight" (iqtataluw) becomes clear, meaning: if one of the two groups begins fighting the other and does not heed reconciliation, then fight the transgressing party.

[Page 240]

Baghy (transgression) means injustice and encroachment upon the right of another. Here it is used in its linguistic sense, which differs from its juristic (fiqhi) sense. So "the one that transgresses" is the unjust group that departs from the truth, even if it has not fought, because its transgression compels the group that is wronged to defend its right.

The ruling on fighting the transgressing party is that it be a group, because it is difficult to restrain the oppression of a large group by individuals or police helpers. Therefore it became necessary to restrain them from transgression with an army and weapons.

This applies to fighting between groups and tribes. As for a faction leaving the community of the Muslims, that is more severe and is not the subject of this verse, but the verse is a foundation for it in legislation.

The people of apostasy (ahl al-riddah) transgressed against the community of the Muslims by a transgression without fighting, and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, fought them. The rebels from among the people of Egypt transgressed against 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, so they were transgressors against the community of the believers. 'Uthman refused to fight them, disliked being the cause of shedding the blood of Muslims, and in his own ijtihad he held that it was obligatory for the Muslims to obey him, since he was the ruler. He did not deny the rebels the description of transgression.

The description of baghy is established by the report of the scholars that one group transgressed against the other, or by the judgment of a knowledgeable and just caliph. It also occurs when one departs from obedience to the caliph and from the community by the sword, if he orders what is not oppressive or tyrannical, and if disobeying him does not lead to strife, because the harm of strife is greater than the harm of tyranny that does not destroy the public interests of the Muslims. This is because departing from obedience to the caliph is transgression against the community that is with the caliph.

The realization of the meaning of baghy and its forms was not fixed in the early period of Islam. The scholars defined it only after the Battle of the Camel, and it did not last long there after the Battle of Siffin. In that battle, the fighting was between two parties, and those who departed from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, were not among those who had pledged allegiance to him for the caliphate. Rather, they had stipulated, as a condition of their pledge to him, that he take retaliation (qawad) from the murderers of 'Uthman among them. So the position of Mu'awiya's companions was a field for ijtihad among them. Books were exchanged between them containing the proofs of both sides, and it is not known which of them is authentic and which is false, since the historians had differing inclinations. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Talhah and al-Zubayr thought it better to begin with killing the murderers of 'Uthman, but after that the scholars verified that the transgression lay on the side of Mu'awiya's companions, because the pledge of allegiance to the caliphate does not accept being restricted by a condition.

[Page 241]

All agree that Mu'awiya and his companions were defending an erroneous ijtihadi view. The obligation required a group of Muslims to call for reconciliation between the two parties, in accordance with the Qur'an's command, as a collective obligation (wujub al-kifayah). It has been said that this call was made but was not completed, because the Kharijites (al-Haruriyyah) broke away over the arbitration (tahkim), saying: "There is no judgment but Allah's," and "We do not accept men as judges."

It was also said that a scheme was devised between the two arbiters. The reports on this are confused, given the differing accounts of the historians who narrated the matter, who had their own inclinations. And Allah knows best what is in hearts.

Al-Hasan al-Basri was asked about the fighting among the Companions and said: "The Companions of Muhammad were present and we were absent, they knew and we were ignorant." Al-Muhasibi said: "You should know that those people were more knowledgeable than us about what they entered into."

The command in His saying ﴿then fight the one that transgresses﴾ is for obligation, because this is a ruling between the two disputants, and judging by the truth is obligatory, since it preserves the right of the one who is right. Also, leaving the transgressing party unfought leads to its continuing in transgression and to the loss of the rights of the wronged party in lives, property, and honor, and Allah does not love corruption. Moreover, that encourages others to do the same. Thus fighting it is a deterrent to others. This is a collective obligation, which becomes specific when the imam appoints an army to fight it. It is not permissible for anyone to take charge of fighting the rebels except the imams and caliphs. When the matter of the imamate is disrupted, the majority of the community and its scholars shall take charge of fighting the rebels. This obligation is absolute in all circumstances, but it is restricted by the evidences indicating that one should not resort to it if it is known that fighting them will lead to a strife greater than their transgression.

The transgressing party may be unclear among the two fighting groups, for the causes of fighting may arise from matters that are not taken seriously at first, and then the flame erupts and both sides clash, so the transgressor between them cannot be identified. Reconciliation between them removes the confusion. If one of them refuses, then transgression is established on its side. For the imam and the judge may compel reconciliation when he fears strife and sees its signs. This is after the doubt of each of the two groups has been made clear to it, if it has any doubt, and is removed by clear proof and decisive evidence. Whoever of them refuses is more disobedient and more unjust.

[Page 242]

He made "the return to the command of Allah" the limit of the fighting, meaning that the fighting against the transgressing group continues until it returns to the command of Allah. The command of Allah is what is in the Shari'ah of justice and restraint from wrongdoing, meaning: until it ceases its transgression. The implied meaning of this limit is then followed by an explanation of how the two groups are to be treated after the transgressing party returns, in His saying ﴿If it returns, then make peace between them justly﴾. The "ba'" here indicates accompaniment, and the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "make peace" (aslihu).

Justice ('adl) is that upon which reconciliation takes place by mutual consent and fairness, and that does not harm either of the two groups. The losses that befall both groups may differ greatly, so it is obligatory to take account of proportion.

He restricted the reconciliation commanded second by the condition "if it returns," with the qualifier "justly," and did not restrict the reconciliation commanded first. This qualifier also applies to the reconciliation commanded first, because a qualifier is naturally drawn back to what it modifies when the cause of the unrestricted and the restricted is the same. Meaning: justice is obligatory in the form of reconciliation, so that the parties do not, under the guise of settlement, waste the benefits of either side, except to the extent that the reality of settlement requires, namely giving up some right in a reasonable way.

Then He commanded the Muslims to act justly generally, by His saying "and act equitably" (aqsitu), as a general command that concludes the specific command of justice in reconciling the two groups. This includes acting justly even while fighting the transgressing party, and then He said: "If it returns, then make peace between them." This is a second reconciliation after the first one commanded at the outset. Its meaning is that the group that submits to force and lays down its weapons will be broken in spirit, feeling the victory of the other group over it. So He obligated the Muslims to reconcile them by encouraging them to remove their grudges and return to the brotherhood of Islam, lest estrangement return between them.

Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: Part of justice in their reconciliation is that they should not be held accountable for what happened between them during the fighting, whether of blood or property, for that is loss under interpretation (ta'wil). Demanding it from them would drive them away from reconciliation and encourage further transgression. This is a principle of public interest. End of quotation.

Then he said: There is no liability for them regarding life or property, according to us (the Malikis). Abu Hanifah said they are liable. For al-Shafi'i there are two opinions. As for what remains in existence, it is returned in its own form. Consider whether Ibn al-'Arabi's statement applies to both kinds of transgressors, or whether it is specific to those who rebel against the caliph, which is the more apparent view.

[Page 243]

As for the ruling on the conduct of the army fighting the rebels, it is like the rulings of jihad, except that their captive is not killed, their fugitive is not pursued, their wounded are not finished off, their families are not taken captive, their property is not seized as spoils, and their prisoners are not enslaved.

For the jurists there are detailed rulings concerning the compensation of the harms that befall the group that was wronged, and the harms that befall the community that undertakes to fight the rebels (bughat). Therefore, from the totality of their opinions one should take what those in authority (ulu al-amr) judge to be in the public interest to impose, in accordance with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And act justly; indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾.

[p. 244]

This is a reason (ta'lil) for establishing reconciliation among the believers when a dispute among them escalates. The sentence therefore functions as a cause, and this reasoning is built on treating the relationship among Muslims as that of brothers.

The restrictive form (qasr), which confines their condition to the condition of brothers, is used to emphasize this ruling among Muslims. It is either a claimed restriction (qasr idda'i) or a specific restriction (qasr idafi), aimed at refuting those in the supposed situation who oppress other believers. He describes them as brothers metaphorically, through an eloquent simile (tashbih baligh), to reinforce the meaning of brotherhood among them, so that it is not permissible to attach to them a particle of comparison, which would imply that their condition falls short of true brotherhood.

This verse provides strong evidence that brotherhood among Muslims is an established obligation, because the function of *innama* (indeed, only) is to introduce a statement that the addressee does not ignore and whose truth he does not deny, or something that takes the place of such a statement. As the Shaykh (al-Jurjani) stated in *Dala'il al-I'jaz* in the twelfth chapter, and cited many examples from the Qur'an and Arabic speech in support of this, the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, the believers are but brothers﴾, indicate that the meaning of brotherhood among them is known and established. This has been confirmed within the discourse of Allah the Exalted and the speech of His Messenger (ﷺ). Among that is the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿They say, "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith"﴾ [al-Hashr: 10] in Surat al-Hashr, which was revealed before this surah, for it is counted as the hundred and second surah, whereas Surat al-Hujurat is counted as the hundred and eighth of the surahs. The Prophet (ﷺ) established brotherhood between the Muhajirun and the Ansar when he arrived in Madinah, and that was the beginning of brotherhood among Muslims. In a hadith: "If I were to take a close friend other than my Lord, I would have taken Abu Bakr." However, the brotherhood of Islam is superior.

In the chapter on marrying minors to adults in Sahih al-Bukhari, it is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) proposed to 'A'isha from Abu Bakr. Abu Bakr said to him: "I am only your brother." He replied: "You are my brother in the religion of Allah and His Book, and she is lawful to me."

In a hadith in Sahih Muslim: "A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim. He does not wrong him, nor forsake him, nor despise him. It is enough evil for a person to despise his Muslim brother."

In a hadith: "None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself," meaning he loves for the Muslim what he loves for himself.

The phrase "﴿Indeed, the believers are but brothers﴾" points to the reason why reconciliation between the two opposing groups among them is obligatory, by showing that faith has established among its adherents a bond of kinship, derived from revelation, that is no less than the bond of physical brotherhood. This is similar to the words of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab to the woman who complained to him about the need of her children and said: "I am the daughter of Khufaf ibn Ayma', and my father witnessed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) al-Hudaybiyya." 'Umar said: "Welcome to a near kinship."

Since it is customary among people that when enmity arises between two brothers, the rest of the brothers must rise to remove it by seeking reconciliation between them, likewise the duty of Muslims, when discord arises between two groups among them, is that the rest of them should strive for reconciliation between them, dispatching envoys, until they mend what has been broken and repair what has been damaged.

The command to reconcile between the two brothers is derived as a consequence of establishing that the believers are brothers. This is a confirmation of the causal meaning implied by *innama*. Thus the command to reconcile, which came initially without a reason in His words ﴿So make peace between them﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], and His words ﴿So make peace between them with justice﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], has been followed by the reason, so its affirmation is achieved, and then it is further supported by a consequence, which strengthens it further.

This arrangement has produced something resembling a claim (da'wa), which is like the thing to be proven in a syllogism (qiyas), then something resembling the proof by analogy, then something resembling the conclusion.

Since the meaning of brotherhood among the believers has been fully established, he departed from saying "So make peace between the two groups" to His words ﴿between your two brothers﴾. This is a new description that arose from His words ﴿Indeed, the believers are but brothers﴾, so its application to the two groups is determined. This is not an instance of placing an apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, so reflect on this.

The dual form is used in His words "your two brothers" in consideration of the fact that the discourse concerns two groups of believers, so each group is treated as a brother to the other.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read "between your two brothers" with the dual form of "brother," meaning between the one group and the other, in consideration of the narrative concerning the fighting of two groups.

Al-Jumhur also read "between your two brothers" with the dual form of "brother," treating each group as a brother.

Ya'qub read "So make peace between your brothers" (fa-aslihu bayna ikhwatikum) with a feminine plural "ta'" after the waw, as the plural of "brother," considering each individual from the two groups as a brother.

The one addressed by His words ﴿And fear Allah that you may receive mercy﴾ is all the believers. It thus includes the two groups, the transgressing one and the one that was wronged, and it includes others besides them who were commanded to reconcile between them and to fight the transgressing group. Each is strengthened by standing at what Allah has commanded each of them concerning what pertains to them. This resembles a concluding statement (tadhyil).

The meaning of ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾ is: mercy from Allah is hoped for you, so that your affairs proceed in uprightness and righteousness. Mercy was chosen because the command to fear Allah comes immediately after establishing the reality of brotherhood among the believers, and the conduct proper to brothers is mercy, so the reward for it is of the same kind.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verse 11:

[Page 246]
﴿O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people, perhaps they are better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women, perhaps they are better than them.﴾
When brotherhood requires that good treatment be given between the two brothers, then what has been established of the obligation of treating brothers well among the Muslims requires good treatment among their individuals. So these verses came to alert [the believers] to matters of good treatment that people are often heedless of, because of how widespread their neglect was in the Jahiliyyah. This is for this occasion. This is the fourth call (nida'), after which the command is to the Muslims concerning the obligation of some courtesy among their members.

From al-Dahhak: the intended people were the Banu Tamim, when they ridiculed Bilal, 'Ammar and Suhayb. So the revelation of the verse has a cause (sabab) connected to the cause for which the surah was revealed, and this is from the ridicule that is forbidden.

Al-Wahidi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the cause of its revelation was: Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas had a hearing impairment, and whenever he came to the gathering of the Prophet ﷺ he would say, "Make room for him so that he can sit beside him and hear what he says." One day he came pushing through the necks of the people, and a man said, "You have found a place, so sit down." Thabit said, "Who is this?" The man said, "I am so-and-so." Thabit said, "The son of so-and-so," and he mentioned a mother of his for whom he used to be reproached in the Jahiliyyah. The man was ashamed, so Allah revealed this verse. This is from the lamz (insulting allusion).

It is narrated from Ikrimah that it was revealed when some of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ reproached Umm Salamah for being short, and this is from ridicule.

It was also said: some of them reproached Safiyyah for being a Jewess, and this is from lamz in their usage.

These verses open with the repetition of the call (nida') for the sake of giving attention to the purpose, so that it stands independently and is not subordinate, as has been stated above from the words of al-Fakhr (al-Razi). The verses that follow this call address an important category of how Muslims treat one another, in which people had become lax since the age of Jahiliyyah. These are harmful statements, and the prohibition of them requires the command of their opposites. These prohibited matters are sukhriyah (ridicule), lamz (insulting allusion) and nabz (derisive nicknaming).

[Page 247]
As for al-sakhr, it is said also al-sukhriyah: mockery (istihza'), and it has been mentioned in His saying ﴿فَيَسْخَرُونَ مِنهم﴾ in Surah Bara'ah, and the reason for its construction with min has been mentioned.

Al-qawm (people) is a collective noun: a group of men specifically, to the exclusion of women. Zuhayr said:

"I do not know, and I will presume to know: are the people of Hisn men, or women?"

The indefinite form qawm in both places serves to convey generality, lest it be supposed that the prohibition concerns specific people who ridiculed specific people.

The reason "yaskhar" is attributed to "qawm" rather than saying "let not some of you ridicule some of you," as in His saying ﴿ولا يَغْتَبْ بَعْضُكم بَعْضًا﴾ [al-Hujurat: 12], is to prohibit what was common among the Arabs, namely the ridicule of tribes by other tribes; so the prohibition was directed at peoples. For this same reason He did not say "let not a man ridicule a man, nor a woman [ridicule] a woman."

From it is understood the prohibition of anyone ridiculing anyone by way of lahn al-khitab (implicit inference). This prohibition is explicit in forbidding it.

Women were singled out for mention even though qawm includes them by way of customary predominance in speech, just as the word "believers" (al-mu'minin) includes believing women in the terminology of the Qur'an, by the context of legislation, since the original basis is equality in rulings, except where evidence requires specifying one of the two categories. This is to repel the supposition that the prohibition is restricted to the ridicule of men, since mockery is rooted in women; so for the sake of repelling this supposition arising from these two faults, [the Qur'an specifies them], in the manner mentioned earlier in His saying in the verse of retaliation ﴿والأُنْثى بِالأُنْثى﴾ [al-Baqarah: 178] in Surah al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿عَسى أنْ يَكُونُوا خَيْرًا مِنهُمْ﴾ is a resumptive, interposed clause between the two conjoined clauses, serving to intensify the prohibition of ridicule by mentioning a state that frequently occurs in the one ridiculed, so that the ridicule of the mocker becomes more monstrous. It also arouses the emotion of shame in the mocker's own soul. The clause "perhaps they are better than them" is not an attribute of "a people" in His saying "a people [ridicule] a people"; otherwise the prohibition of ridicule would be specific to cases where the one ridiculed is presumed to be better than the mocker. The same applies to the clause "perhaps they are better than them" [referring to women], and it is not an attribute of "women" in "women [ridicule] women."

[Page 248]
The similarity of the two pronouns in His saying ﴿أنْ يَكُونُوا خَيْرًا مِنهُمْ﴾ and in His saying ﴿أنْ يَكُنَّ خَيْرًا مِنهُنَّ﴾ is not ambiguous, since the referent of each pronoun is clear. It is like the pronouns in His saying "and they cultivated it more than they cultivated it" in Surah al-Rum, and in the saying of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"We returned, and had we not been [here], their host would have surrounded the Muslims, and they would have secured what they had gathered."

* * *
﴿And do not defame one another, nor call each other by nicknames.﴾
Al-lamz: mentioning what the speaker considers a fault in someone, to his face; it is direct confrontation with what is disliked. If it is true, it is rudeness and transgression; if it is false, it is rudeness and lying. It was common among the Arabs in their Jahiliyyah. Allah said: ﴿ويْلٌ لِكُلِّ هُمَزَةٍ لُمَزَةٍ﴾ [al-Humazah: 1], meaning a group of polytheists whose practice was to defame the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It may take the form of a state between gesture and speech, by moving the two lips with a low speech from which the one addressed understands that he is being blamed or threatened, or belittled, in many possible ways. It is other than nabz and other than backbiting (ghibah).

The exegetes and lexicographers differ in explaining the meaning of lamz, and what I have mentioned is what has been extracted as the correct sense of it.

The meaning of "﴿and do not defame yourselves﴾" is: let not some of you defame others, so the defamed party is treated as the self of the one who defames him, because of the established meaning of brotherhood. Its parallel has been mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿ولا تُخْرِجُونَ أنْفُسَكم مِن دِيارِكُمْ﴾ [al-Baqarah: 84] in Surah al-Baqarah.

Al-tanabuz: calling one another by nicknames. Al-nabz with a sukun on the ba' is the mention of nabaz, with a fatha on the ba', which is the bad nickname, like their saying "anf al-naqah" (nose of the she-camel), "qurqur," and "battah" (duck). Most of the nicknames in the Jahiliyyah were nabz. A man of the Banu Fazarah said:

"I call him by a kunyah when I call him, to honour him, and I do not give him a laqab, and the evil is the laqab."

It is narrated with the nominative "al-sau'ah al-laqab" (the evil is the nickname), which follows the more common usage among them, that a nickname is an evil. It is also narrated as "al-sau'ah" in the accusative, taking the waw as the waw of accompaniment. And it is narrated as "bil-sau'ati al-laqaba," meaning: I do not give him a nickname that accompanies evil, so he intends avoiding some nicknames, which indicate badness. The nominative narration is more preferred, and it is what Sibawayh's citation of a line after it in the chapter on zanna requires. Perhaps what occurred in the Diwan al-Hamasah of changes by Abu Tammam, some of which were attributed to him in some lines of the Hamasah, is because he saw the accusative as more correct in meaning.

So the word "al-alqab" (nicknames) in the verse means the disliked nicknames, by the context of "﴿and do not call each other by nicknames﴾."

A laqab is that which suggests lowliness or nobility, whether the person is called by it or whether the one who coins it for him invents it.

The prohibition in the verse has been restricted to those nicknames whose age has not lasted so long that they have become like the names of their bearers, and the intention of disparagement and abuse has been forgotten. It is specified by what occurred in many hadiths, such as the Prophet's ﷺ saying "Dhu al-Yadayn spoke truly," and his saying to Abu Hurayrah: "O Abu Hirr." Shawul, king of Israel, was called Talut in the Qur'an, and the scholars' saying "al-A'raj" to 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hurmuz and "al-A'mash" to Sulayman ibn Mihran.

He said "﴿and do not defame﴾" in the form of the verb arising from one side, and He said "﴿and do not call one another by nicknames﴾" in the form of the verb arising from two sides, because lamz occurs rarely, whereas it was common in the Jahiliyyah among many tribes, including the Banu Salimah in Medina, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said.
