﴿How wicked is the name of wickedness after faith. And whoever does not repent, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾
This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the prohibitions mentioned earlier, and it is a strong allusion that what they were forbidden from is wickedness (fusuq) and wrongdoing (zulm). Without the sense of allusion that this is wickedness, and that it is blameworthy and punishable, there would be no connection between the meaning of this sentence and the sentences before it. His saying ﴿بِئْسَ الِاسْمُ الفُسُوقُ بَعْدَ الإيمانِ﴾ indicates that what they were forbidden from is blameworthy, because it is wickedness for which one is punished, and which is removed only by repentance. So there is brevity by omitting two sentences from the speech, relying on what the concluding statement indicates. This shows that lamz and tanabuz are two disobediences, because they are wickedness. In a hadith: "Abusing a Muslim is wickedness."

The word "ism" (name) here is used absolutely for mention, that is, naming, as one says: "his name flew among the people for generosity or for baseness." The meaning is: how wicked is the mention by which someone is described with wickedness after he has been described with faith.

The choice of the word "ism" here is well-placed in eloquence, because the context is a warning against mentioning people by blameworthy names, since nicknames are names; so choosing the word "ism" for wickedness is a semantic parallelism.

The meaning of "after" in His saying ﴿بَعْدَ الإيمانِ﴾ is: after being characterized by faith. That is, faith does not suit wickedness, because sins are the characteristic of the people of polytheism, who are not restrained from wickedness by any restrainer. This is like the saying of Jamilah bint Ubayy when she complained to the Prophet ﷺ that she disliked her husband Thabit ibn Qays and came seeking separation from him: "I do not fault Thabit in religion or in character, but I dislike disbelief after Islam" (she intends an allusion to fear of fornication), "and I cannot endure him in hatred."

Since each of ridicule, lamz and tanabuz is a disobedience, repentance from them is obligatory. Whoever does not repent is a wrongdoer: he wronged people by transgressing against them, and wronged himself by accepting for it the punishment of the Hereafter while able to desist from that. So his wrongdoing is very severe. Therefore the restrictive form of the wrongdoers is applied to them, as if there were no wrongdoers other than them, since the other wrongdoers are not counted in comparison with these, for the sake of emphasis, so that they may be restrained.

Repentance is obligatory from every sin, and these mentioned sins are of different degrees; persistence in minor sins amounts to a major sin.

The placement of the demonstrative (ism al-ishara, "those") serves to increase their distinction, to make their condition appear dreadful, and to draw attention. Rather, they deserve the restriction of wrongdoing to themselves because of the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative.

[Page 250 continues]

﴿O you who believe, avoid much suspicion, for indeed some suspicion is sin﴾

The address was repeated for the fifth time because the purposes differ and because of the importance given to the matter. The prohibitions mentioned after this address are of the kind of bad dealings that are hidden, so that the one who is treated thus does not perceive them, and therefore does not repel them. Nothing removes them from the heart of the one who treats another this way.

[Page 251]

In the words of the Exalted: ﴿avoid much suspicion﴾ there is a great discipline that nullifies what was widespread in the Jahiliyyah (the period of ignorance before Islam) of evil suspicions and baseless accusations. Evil suspicions give rise to excessive jealousy, plots, assassinations, slander against lineages, and initiating fighting out of fear of an aggression that is merely suspected on baseless conjecture, as they said: "Seize the thief before he seizes you."

Misguided creeds and false doctrines have arisen only from false suspicions. The Exalted said: ﴿They think about God other than the truth, the thought of the Jahiliyyah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 154]. He also said: ﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have no knowledge of that; they only guess﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 20]. He said: ﴿Those who associated partners with God will say: "If God had willed, we would not have associated partners, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything"﴾ [al-An'am: 148]. Then He said: ﴿Say: "Do you have any knowledge that you can produce for us? You only follow conjecture, and you only guess"﴾ [al-An'am: 148].

The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of speech."

When the command in this verse to avoid much suspicion came, we learned that sinful suspicions are not few, so it became obligatory to scrutinise and examine in order to distinguish false suspicion from true suspicion.

By "suspicion" (zann) here is meant the suspicion concerning the conditions of people. The object of the verb was omitted so that the listener's mind goes to every possible suspicion that is a sin.

The clause ﴿indeed some suspicion is sin﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani), because the words ﴿avoid much suspicion﴾ make the listener pause and seek clarification: know that some suspicion is a crime. This is a metaphor (kinayah) for the obligation to reflect on the consequences of suspicions, so that they may place what suspicions lead to against what they know of the rulings of the Shari'ah, or ask the people of knowledge. This explanatory clause is limited to warning against falling into sin. This explanation is not a clarification of the kinds of the "much" suspicion that is commanded to be avoided, for these are many kinds. Rather, it draws attention to its outcome and leaves the detail, because leaving it vague prompts greater caution.

The meaning of its being a sin is that: either a deed arises from that suspicion, or it is merely a belief. If a deed such as backbiting, spying, or other things may arise from it, then let the one who suspects assume that his suspicion is false, and then look at the deed he has built upon it. He will find that he has treated with it someone who does not deserve that treatment, by accusing him falsely; so he sins for what he has harboured in his heart against his Muslim brother. The scholars have said: a bad suspicion about someone whose outward state is good is not permissible.

[Page 252]

If the suspicion gives rise to nothing but a mere belief without deed, then let him assume that his suspicion was mistaken. He will find that he has come to believe something about someone that is not in him. If it is a belief about the attributes of God, then he has slandered God. If it is a belief about the conditions of people, then he has lost the benefit of one he suspected to be harmful, or the guidance of one he suspected to be misguided, or the acquisition of knowledge from one he suspected to be ignorant, and the like.

Beyond this: a false suspicion, when its consideration is repeated and its circulation in the soul is renewed, may become firmly established knowledge in the soul, so consequences follow from it with ease, and it may strike someone who truly deserves the opposite, as has been explained in the words of the Exalted: ﴿lest you harm a people in ignorance and then become regretful for what you have done﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6].

Al-ijtinab (avoidance) is a reflexive form (ifti'al) from jannabahu and ajnabahu, meaning he removed him, i.e. made him a side other than oneself. Its verb takes two objects; one says: jannabahu al-sharr (he kept the evil away from him). The Exalted said: ﴿And keep me and my sons far from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35]. Its intransitive counterpart is ajtanib, meaning I keep away. No imperative of it has been heard except in the reflexive form (ifti'al).

The meaning of the command to avoid much suspicion is the command to take up the means of avoiding it, since suspicion arises in a person's thought involuntarily, by compulsion, not by choice. So it is not rationally conceivable to impose a duty to avoid it outright. What is intended is the command to be firm regarding it, to examine it, and to doubt its truth until its requirement becomes clear without hesitation or with preponderance, or until its falsehood becomes clear, so that you disbelieve yourself in what it has told you.

This warning is meant to resist evil suspicions by means of the sound indicators that are their criterion. In a hadith: "When you suspect, do not verify."

Moreover, a good suspicion that has no basis is not praiseworthy, because it may lead to falling into what cannot be limited in harm, such as delusion in a place where caution is needed, or imitating someone who is not fit to be emulated. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Umm 'Atiyyah when 'Uthman ibn Maz'un died in her house, and she said: "May God's mercy be upon you, Abu al-Sa'ib; my testimony for you is that God has honoured you." He said: "How do you know that God has honoured him?" She said: "O Messenger of God, who then will God honour?" He said: "As for him, certainty has come to him, and I hope good for him, but by God, though I am the Messenger of God, I do not know what will be done with me." Umm 'Atiyyah then said: "By God, I will never again declare anyone pure after him."

It is known from the words ﴿much﴾ and from its clarification by the statement ﴿indeed some suspicion is sin﴾ that some suspicion is not sin. We have not been commanded to avoid the suspicion that is not sin, because "much" is a descriptive term, and its implication by contrary inference (mafhum al-mukhalafah) indicates that the much suspicion we were not commanded to avoid is what is clarified by ﴿indeed some suspicion is sin﴾, meaning that some suspicion is not sin. So the Muslim must take as his criterion for distinguishing one of the two suspicions from the other that he presents it to what the Shari'ah has clarified within its rulings from the Book and the Sunnah, what the community's scholars have agreed upon, what sound ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) has yielded, and the pursuit of the objectives of the Shari'ah. Among suspicions, some must be followed, such as caution against the enemy's plots in war, and the suspicion grounded in evidence derived from the indications of the legal sources, for most legal derivations arise from suspicion grounded in evidence.

The implication of this verse has opened the door to acting on suspicion that is not sinful, though it does not stand as proof except for those who hold that acting on contrary inference (mafhum al-mukhalafah, the argument that what is not stated has the opposite ruling) is valid, and that is the strongest view, since most of the indications of the Arabic language regarding such implications are as established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

As for the suspicion which is a person's understanding and acuity, that is a thought in his own mind, and he is best aware of it, for it is his habit, whether it hits or misses. Aws ibn Hajar said:

"The shrewd one who suspects you with suspicion, as if he had seen and heard."

* * *

﴿And do not spy﴾. Spying is one of the effects of suspicion, because suspicion prompts it when the suspecting self calls him to verify what he has suspected in secret, so he takes the path of investigation. God warned them against taking this path for verification, so that they may take another path, if verifying what was suspected has any benefit. Spying (tajassus) is seeking out by a hidden means, and it is derived from jass (touching), from which the word for spy (jasus) is named.

Spying is a dealing hidden from the one who is spied upon. The reason for the prohibition is that it is a kind of

[Page 253]

plotting and an attempt to peer into the private matters (al-'awrat). The spy may see from the one spied upon what displeases him, and thereby enmity and resentment arise. His chest is oppressed with constriction and fear, after his inner conscience was pure and good; and that is from the misery of life.

This is a breach of Islamic brotherhood, because it prompts the display of hostility. Then if the one who is spied upon discovers the other's spying, it displeases him, and dislike for him arises in his soul, and brotherhood is breached by another breach, as we described in the case of the spy. Then this prompts both to take revenge upon their brother.

Since the prohibition of spying has been considered among the branches of the prohibition of suspicion, it is restricted to the spying which is a sin or leads to sin. When it is known that it leads to a general harm, spying becomes a major sin. Among this is spying on Muslims by someone who seeks to harm them.

So what is prohibited is the spying from which no benefit accrues to the Muslims, nor the warding off of harm from them. Thus it does not include spying on enemies, nor the police spying on criminals and thieves.

* * *

﴿And let not some of you backbite others. Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? You would hate it﴾. Backbiting (ightiab) is a reflexive form from ghabahu (he transgressed or spoke ill of), when one mentions someone in his absence with what displeases him.

So backbiting is mentioning an absent person with what he would not like to be mentioned with. The noun from it is ghibah, with a kasra on the ghayn, like ghilah. Mentioning someone with what he dislikes is backbiting only if what is said does not damage his honour; otherwise it becomes slander (qadh').

The words ﴿And let not some of you backbite others﴾ were used instead of saying "avoid backbiting," for the purpose of preparing the way for the image that follows in ﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾. Because that image includes the sides of the one who backbites and the one who is backbitten, it prepares for it by indicating two persons, because this makes the image clearer.

The interrogative in ﴿Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother?﴾ is affirmative (taqriri), to establish that everyone acknowledges that he does not like that. For this reason the interrogative is answered by the words "﴿You would hate it﴾."

It was not phrased as a negation of liking that, such as "Would none of you like?", as is usual with the affirmative interrogative, to indicate that the acknowledgment imposed on the one addressed is established, so that the one being asked has no room not to acknowledge, and yet he can only acknowledge. Backbiting is represented by eating the flesh of a dead brother, and this implies representing the one who indulges in it as one who likes to eat the flesh of a dead brother. The image aims at making the one represented appear monstrous and repugnant, to convey harshness towards those who backbite, because backbiting is widespread among people, especially in the days of the Jahiliyyah.

Thus the condition of backbiting a Muslim who is one's brother in Islam, while he is absent, is compared to the condition of eating the flesh of one's brother who is dead and cannot defend himself. This image of the form is capable of being divided, so that the one who backbites is likened to an eater of flesh, the one who is backbitten is likened to a brother, and his backbiting is likened to death.

The fa' in the words "﴿You would hate it﴾" is the eloquent fa' (fa' al-fasihah), which indicates that the thing has been stated implicitly, and the pronoun of the absent refers either to "one of you" or to "flesh."

Hatred here means revulsion and disgust. The sense is: if this happens, or if this occurs to you, then you have surely hated it.

The eloquent fa' indicates obligation with what follows it, as al-Zamakhshari stated in his commentary on the words of the Exalted: ﴿They have indeed called you liars by what you say﴾ [al-Furqan: 19], in Surat al-Furqan. That is, it indicates that the one addressed has no escape from committing to the meaning of the answer to its conditional clause, which is omitted.

The meaning is: then it is required that you acknowledge what you were asked about, the one represented by the image (it being impossible to deny it), and your hatred of it and disgust at it are established; so let it also be established that you hate its counterpart, the one represented, which is backbiting. It is as if it were said: "Then hate the one represented just as you hated the one by whom it was represented."

In this statement there are several intensifications. Among them is the affirmative interrogative, which is not used except for something that is accepted by the addressee; so placing a thing within the scope of an affirmative interrogative implies that you claim the addressee does not deny it.

Among them is making the thing that is most hated by the soul the object of the verb of liking, to convey the monstrousness of

[Page 254]

the condition of what is compared to it and of the one who chooses it for himself. For this reason he did not say, "Would any of you bear that he eat the flesh of his dead brother?" but rather, "Would any of you like?"

Among its features is the attribution of the verb to "one of you" (aḥad), to indicate that neither of the two would like it.

Another is that the verse does not stop at likening backbiting to eating the flesh of a human being, but makes the one backbited about a brother.

Another is that it does not stop at the eaten flesh being that of a brother, but makes the brother dead.

Among its rhetorical embellishments is the antithesis (ṭibāq) between "Would one of you like" (*ayuḥibbu*) and "you would hate it" (*fakarihtumūhu*).

Backbiting (ghība) is forbidden, by the evidence of this verse and of reports from the Sunnah, some of which are authentic and some of which are weaker.

This is because it involves the corruption of weakening the bond of Islamic brotherhood. It may also reach the one who is backbitten, so that hostility toward the one who backbit him takes root in his soul, and the structure of brotherhood is damaged. Furthermore, it involves occupying oneself with the affairs of people, and this distracts a person from occupying himself with what is important and beneficial to him, and from leaving aside what does not concern him.

Among the Mālikiyya (the Mālikī school), it is one of the major sins (kabā'ir), though few have stated this explicitly. However, Shaykh ʿAlī al-Ṣaʿīdī, in his gloss on *al-Kifāya*, stated explicitly that among "us" (the Mālikīs) it is a major sin without qualification. The basis for this is that Allah forbade it and denounced it strongly. The apparent implication of the words of al-Sijilmāsī in *Kitāb al-ʿAmal al-Fāsī* is that it is a major sin.

The Shāfiʿiyya (the Shāfiʿī school) classified it among the minor sins (ṣaghā'ir), because the major sin (kabīra), in their terminology, is an act that indicates little concern on the part of its doer for religion and a weakness of religious commitment. This is how Imam al-Haramayn defined it.

If backbiting is for a valid benefit, such as discrediting witnesses and transmitters of hadith, or what is said to one who seeks advice regarding association or marriage, then that is not backbiting, provided that it does not exceed the limit necessary to convey the condition of the person about whom one is asked.

Likewise, there is no backbiting regarding a dissolute person (fāsiq) when one mentions his wickedness without his openly displaying it. The Prophet ﷺ said, when permission was sought for ʿUyayna ibn Ḥiṣn to enter his presence, "Wretched is the brother of the clan," so that whoever heard him would be wary of him, since ʿUyayna at that time had deviated from Islam.

[Page 257]

It is reported from al-Ṭabarī, author of *al-ʿUdda* in the furūʿ (positive law) of the Shāfiʿiyya, that it is a minor sin. Al-Maḥallī said, and al-Rāfiʿī and those who followed him affirmed this. I say: al-Sijilmāsī mentioned in his versified work on the matters on which the judges of Fez had acted:

"Do not disqualify a witness by backbiting, for it has afflicted many with calamity."

He mentioned in its commentary that the judges acted in accordance with the words of al-Ghazālī.

As for the prevalence of an affliction (ʿumūm al-balwā), it does not necessitate overlooking what has become widespread except in cases of necessity and inability, as this was related from Abū Muḥammad ibn Abī Zayd.

In my view, the governing principle is that it must become so common among people that it no longer indicates contempt for the religious restraint, and then the meaning of weakness of religious commitment, which the Shāfiʿiyya made a part of the essence of backbiting, no longer applies to it.

* * *

﴿And fear Allah; indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance, Most Merciful.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the preceding imperative clauses, beginning from His words, ﴿Avoid much suspicion﴾. This is in the manner of a concluding summary (tadhyīl) for them, since He commanded taqwā (God-consciousness), which comprises both avoidance and compliance. Whoever is free from involvement in those prohibited things, the command to taqwā keeps him from becoming involved in any of them in the future. Whoever is already involved in them, or in some of them, the command to taqwā encompasses the command to restrain from what he is involved in.

The clause ﴿indeed, Allah is Accepting of repentance, Most Merciful﴾ is a concluding summary of the concluding summary. This is because taqwā may take the form of repentance after involvement in sin, so He said ﴿indeed Allah is Accepting of repentance﴾. And taqwā may be undertaken from the outset, in which case Allah shows mercy to the one who is God-conscious. Thus, "the Most Merciful" encompasses everyone.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verse 13 (part 1 of 2):

[p. 258]
﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.﴾
This is a transition from the duties of dealings (mu'amalat) to what a person must observe regarding himself. The address is repeated for the sake of emphasis on this purpose, since the pride of each tribe in its own virtues and its preference of its people over others was widespread in the Jahiliyyah, as you see its remnants in the poetry of al-Farazdaq and Jarir. Some tribes were held in contempt, such as Bahila, Dubay'a, and the Banu 'Ukl.

A bedouin was asked: "Would you like to enter Paradise while you are a Bahili?" He lowered his head for a while and then said: "On condition that the people of Paradise do not know that I am a Bahili." Such attitudes lead to grudges and fighting, and from them branch mockery, insulting, nicknaming, suspicion, spying, and backbiting, to which the preceding verses refer. So this verse came to discipline the believers to avoid what was in the Jahiliyyah, to uproot its remaining roots in souls, because the strata of believers had mixed after the year of the delegations (sanat al-wufud), when many entered Islam.

Abu Dawud related in his book al-Marasil, from al-Zuhri, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered the Banu Bayada of the Ansar that they should marry Abu Hind (a freedman of the Banu Bayada, it is said his name was Yasar) to a woman from among them. They said: 'Do you marry our daughters to our clients?' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have created you from male and female and made you peoples...﴾" — the verse. Other reports have been related regarding its occasion of revelation.

They were addressed with the designation "mankind" rather than "the believers," in keeping with the relevance between this designation and what the purpose opened with, namely the reminder that their origin is one, that is, that they are equal in creation, so that through this one reaches the conclusion that superiority and boasting are only by virtues, and that superiority in Islam is by increase in taqwa. Thus it was said: ﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female.﴾

As for one who holds that this verse was revealed in Makkah apart from the rest of the surah, he is deceived by the fact that most of the address with ﴿O mankind﴾ occurred in the Makki surahs.

What is meant by "male and female" is Adam and Eve, the two parents of humanity, by the indication of His saying ﴿and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another.﴾

[p. 259]
This is supported by the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "You are the children of Adam, and Adam is from dust," as will come shortly. Thus the tanwin of ﴿male and female﴾ is for them being two attributes of a qualified noun, and so it is determined: that is, from a male father and a female mother.

It is also possible that what is meant by "male and female" is the category of male and the category of female, i.e., each one is formed from the category of male and female.

The particle min (from) in both possibilities is for origin (ibtida').

Shu'ub (peoples) is the plural of sha'b, with a fatha on the shin, and it is the gathering of tribes that trace back to one common ancestor from a particular nation; it is sometimes called jadhm. Thus the Arab nation divides into many peoples: Mudar is a people, Rabi'a is a people, Anmar is a people, Iyad is a people; and the Arab nation, the Musta'ribah, which is 'Adnan from the descendants of Isma'il (peace be upon him), together with Himyar and Saba', and al-Azd, are peoples of the nation of Qahtan. Kinana, Qays, and Tamim are tribes of the people of Mudar. Madhhij and Kinda are two tribes of the people of Saba'. Al-Aws and al-Khazraj are two tribes of the people of al-Azd.

Under the tribe is the 'imara, such as Quraysh from Kinana; under the 'imara is the batn, such as Qusayy from Quraysh; under the batn is the fakhdh, such as Hashim and Umayya from Qusayy; under the fakhdh is the fasila, such as Abu Talib, al-'Abbas, and Abu Sufyan.

He limited mention to peoples and tribes because what is beneath them is included by way of implicit meaning (lahn al-khitab).

The Qur'an passed over mention of the nations, following what is customary in the speech of the Arabs in dividing the strata of lineages, since they only recognize their own lineages.

The cause of Allah's making them peoples and tribes is stated, and His wisdom in this making is that people may know one another, i.e., some of them know others.

Knowing (ta'aruf) occurs in layers after layers, progressing upward: the single family know one another, the clan (in'ashira) consists of people who know one another from families, since they are not free of kinship and marriage ties; and so clans know one another with the batns, the batns with the 'amā'ir, the 'amā'ir with the tribes, and the tribes with the peoples, because every rank is composed of the totality of the ranks beneath it.

[p. 260]
This division, which Allah inspired in them, was a firm system for binding their ties without hardship or impossibility, for facilitating the accomplishment of work among a widely dispersed number is achieved by dividing its acquisition among a small number, then by spreading its work among groups of that small number, then between it and larger groups. Thus it continues until it covers a nation or all people. Civilizations similar among humans have spread only by this wise law.

The intended meaning is: you have distorted the natural disposition (fitra) and reversed the situation, making the difference of peoples and tribes a cause of mutual repudiation, strife, and aggression.

Do you not see the saying of al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas ibn 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab:

"Gently, sons of our paternal uncles, gently, our clients;
Do not stir up between us what was buried."
"Do not expect that you can belittle us while we honor you,
And that we restrain harm from you while you harm us."

And the saying of al-'Uqayli, when his paternal cousins fought him and he killed some of them:

"We weep when we kill you, over you,
And we kill you as if we did not care."

And the saying of al-Shamidhar al-Harithi:

"It has displeased me what war has dragged between us,
O sons of our paternal uncle, had it been a matter that could be remedied."

Their sayings on this are beyond counting, besides what is below that of boasting, arrogance, mockery, insulting, nicknaming, evil suspicion, and backbiting already mentioned.

Allah has mended the breach of the Arabs through Islam, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you, when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together, so you became, by His favor, brothers﴾ [Al 'Imran: 103], returning them to the natural disposition upon which He created them. Likewise, the turns of the Islamic religion return people to the sound disposition.

When Allah, the Exalted, commanded the believers to be brothers and to reconcile between the warring factions, and forbade them what breaks brotherhood and what tarnishes its light in their souls: mockery, insulting, mutual nicknaming, evil suspicion, spying, and backbiting, He reminded them of the origin of brotherhood in lineages, which the brotherhood of Islam and the unity of belief have reinforced, so that this reminder would be an aid to their insight into their condition.

[p. 261]
And since mockery, insulting, and nicknaming are things that rivalry between individuals and tribes drives to, Allah gathered all of that in this wise admonition, which indicates by way of address to them that they resorted to this division which divine wisdom established and used it for its corrupt implications, neglecting the good purpose for which it was made, by His saying "that you may know one another." Then He followed it with His saying: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you,﴾ meaning: if you compete, then compete in taqwa, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And for this let the competitors compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 26].

The statement in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have created you from male and female﴾ is used figuratively (kinaya) for equality in the origin of the human species, so that from this one may arrive at the desire to acquire the virtues and excellences that raise some people above others, by a figure of two degrees (kinaya bi-martabatayn). The meaning intended from this is the content of the clause ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾. That clause stands, relative to the clause ﴿Indeed, We have created you from male and female﴾, in the position of the purpose relative to the premise and of the conclusion relative to the syllogism, and therefore it was separated (fusila) because it is in the position of explanation (bayan).

As for the clause ﴿and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another﴾, it is parenthetical (mu'tarida) between the other two clauses.

The purpose of its parenthetical insertion is to incorporate (idmaj) another discipline, from the duty of spreading acquaintance and communication among tribes and nations, and that this is what Allah wants from them.

Among the meaning of the verse is what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed in the Farewell Pilgrimage when he said: "O people, indeed your Lord is one, and your father is one. There is no superiority of an Arab over a non-Arab, nor of a non-Arab over an Arab, nor of a black person over a red person, nor of a red person over a black person, except by taqwa."

And from the pattern of the verse's composition and its clarification is what al-Tirmidhi related in his tafsir of this verse, the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah has removed from you the arrogance of the Jahiliyyah and its pride. [People are] of two kinds: a believing, pious person, or a wicked, miserable sinner. You are the children of Adam, and Adam is from dust." In another narration, it is that this was among what he addressed on the day of the Conquest of Makkah. ('Ubbiyya, with a damma on the ayn (unpointed letter) or a kasra, and with a shadda on the subsequent muwahhada (b) with a kasra, then a shadda on the yaʼ with two dots below: arrogance and pride. Its measure, according to the dialect with a damma on the fa, is fu'ulliyya, and according to the dialect with a kasra on the fa, is fi'liyya. It is either derived from ta'biya (preparation), so the doubling of the ba is merely for augmentation, like nadda al-thawb meaning nada (to be wet/soaked), or it is derived from 'uban al-ma' (surge of water), so the doubling in the ba is original.)

[p. 262]
In a narration of Ibn Abi Hatim, with his chain to Ibn 'Umar: "The Messenger of Allah circumambulated on the day of the Conquest of Makkah, then addressed them in the valley of al-Musayyil," and he mentioned the hadith, adding that Allah says: ﴿O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female﴾ up to ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted.﴾

The clause ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ is a fresh, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i). It was placed later in the arrangement than the clause "﴿Indeed, We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another﴾," so that that preceding clause would serve as a preparation for this one and stand in relation to it as a premise. For when they were equal in the origin of creation, from one father and one mother, the matter was that one should not excel another except by perfection of the soul, which is the perfection that Allah is pleased with for them, and which He made taqwa its means. For this reason He attached superiority in nobility to "in the sight of Allah," since there is no regard for nobility that Allah does not heed.

What is meant by "the most noble" (akram) is the most precious and most honored, as its explanation has preceded in His saying ﴿Indeed, a noble letter has been delivered to me﴾ [al-Naml: 29] in Surat al-Naml.

"Al-atqa" (the most righteous) is the one most excellent in taqwa, and it is a superlative formed from ittaqa irregularly.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Acquainted﴾ gives the reason for the content of ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾: that is, the most noble of you was the most righteous because Allah is Knowing of true nobility, while you have made nobility lie in what is beneath that, in tyranny, squandering wealth without cause, and other things; the nobility which is taqwa, He is Acquainted with the measure of people's portions of taqwa, so these are, in His sight, the portions of nobility. Therefore the most noble is the most righteous. This is like His saying: ﴿So do not attribute purity to yourselves; He knows best who has taqwa﴾ [al-Najm: 32], meaning He knows best your ranks in taqwa, which is the true purification. From this category is His saying (﴿Allah knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]).

It is known that His saying ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ does not preclude that people may have other nobilities in a second rank after taqwa, of the kind that has an effect of purification on souls, such as good upbringing, purity of lineage, distinction in knowledge and civilization, good reputation among nations and in tribes and in families, and likewise according to what authentic history has perpetuated for nations and individuals. For what leaves traces in its members and qualities in its descendants. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "People are mines like the mines of gold and silver; the best of them in the Jahiliyyah are the best of them in Islam, when they gain understanding."

For in the character of children there are traces of the natures of fathers, lower or higher, which make their souls prepared for perfection or its opposite. Upbringing and training have considerable effects in perfecting or diminishing souls, and customs and traditions have their effects in elevation and abasement. All of these are means of preparing souls for perfection and the true purity which taqwa lays out.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir), surah 49, verse 13 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware﴾ is a tadhyil (a concluding clause that reinforces the preceding meaning with a general truth), and it is a kinaya (an indirect expression) for the command to purify their intentions in their dealings and in what they seek of taqwa (God-consciousness), in that Allah knows what is in their souls and will hold them to account for it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verse 14:

﴿The Bedouins say, "We have believed." Say, "You have not believed; but say, 'We have submitted,' for faith has not yet entered your hearts. And if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not deprive you [the reward] of your deeds at all. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾

It was among the delegations that came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the year nine, called the Year of Delegations, the delegation of the Banu Asad ibn Khuzayma. They used to dwell near Madina, and their coming to Madina followed the coming of the delegation of the Banu Tamim that is mentioned at the beginning of the surah. The Banu Asad came in a large number, and among them were Dirar ibn al-Azwar and Tulayha ibn 'Abd Allah, who claimed prophethood after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ) during the apostasy (al-Ridda). This year was a year of drought in their lands, so they embraced Islam. They used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ): "The Arabs have come to you with themselves upon the backs of their mounts, and we have come to you with our baggage, our dependants and our offspring, and we did not fight you as the warriors of Khasafa, Hawazin and Ghatafan fought you." They would come to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and go away with this statement, and they would act as if they were doing him a favour, and they wanted him to direct the charities (sadaqat) toward them. So Allah revealed these verses concerning them, up to the end of the surah, because the two stories occurred in close succession: the story of the delegation of the Banu Tamim and the story of the delegation of the Banu Asad. The purposes of the rudeness they are characterised by are similar. Al-Suddi said: it was revealed concerning the Bedouins mentioned in Surat al-Fath in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The ones who lagged behind among the Bedouins will say to you, "Our wealth and our families kept us busy"﴾ [al-Fath: 11], and so on to the verse.

They said "We have believed" so that they would be secure concerning their lives and their property; when they were called to march to al-Hudaybiya they held back, so this verse was revealed.

Al-A'rab (the Bedouins): the inhabitants of the desert among the Arabs. I think that it is not applied to the desert-dwellers who are not Arabs. It is a collective noun with no singular form of its own, so the individual member is called a'rabi, with the relative ya' (ya' al-nisba).

The definition of al-A'rab here is the definite of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), referring to specific Bedouins, namely the Banu Asad. Therefore this ruling in the verse does not apply strictly to all the inhabitants of the deserts, nor did anyone other than the Banu Asad say this statement.

They said "We have believed" when they were in doubt; faith had not yet taken firm root in them. So Allah informed them of what was in their hearts and made them know that faith is the affirmation of the heart, not merely of the tongue, with the aim that they would become sincere and firmly establish it, as He explained after this verse with His saying: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat: 15], up to the verse.

The concession (al-istidrak) with the particle (lakin, "but") serves to remove what might be suspected from His saying "You have not believed": that they came intending to betray the Prophet (ﷺ). He said ﴿but say, "We have submitted"﴾ only to teach them the difference between faith (iman) and Islam, for Islam is established by the tongue and by the bodily acts, which are the four pillars of Islam: the prayer, the zakat, the fasting of Ramadan and the pilgrimage to the Ka'ba. This is in the hadith of 'Umar about Jibril's questioning of the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning Islam, iman, ihsan and the Hour. Islam is: "That you testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, establish the prayer, pay the zakat, fast Ramadan, and make the pilgrimage to the House if you are able to make your way to it." So when these Bedouins came displaying Islam while their hearts were not at rest in the articles of faith, because they were recent in their acquaintance with it, Allah refuted their statement "We have believed," so that they would know that their inner state is not hidden from Allah, and that Islam is not accounted valid unless faith accompanies it. Neither one suffices without the other: faith without Islam is stubbornness, and Islam without faith is hypocrisy, and obedience to Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) unites them.

The apparent structure of the speech would have been: "Say: you have not believed, but you have submitted," or: "Say: do not say 'we have believed', but say 'we have submitted'," so that the conceded element and the concession correspond according to the familiar arrangement in disputations. He deviated from the apparent form to this arrangement because in it there is an explicit negation of faith from them, so they do not suppose that they deceived the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

By His saying "You have not believed" the expression "do not say 'we have believed'" was dispensed with, because it is offensive to address them with a wording whose sense is a prohibition against announcing faith, since they are required to believe and to say "We have believed" as a truthful statement, not a false one. So it was said to them "You have not believed," as a rebuke to them, without explicitly using the word "rebuke"; but an allusion to this occurred afterwards in His saying: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, then they did not doubt﴾ [al-Hujurat: 15], up to His saying: ﴿Those are the truthful﴾ [al-Hujurat: 15], meaning: not you. For this reason the concession was brought in, understood as carrying the meaning.

He deviated from saying "but you have submitted" to "say 'we have submitted'" as an allusion to the obligation of truthfulness in speech, so that it corresponds to reality. They feel that their lie has become apparent, and that is something to be ashamed of; that is, the proper course is that you say a truthful statement.

His saying ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in "you have not believed", and it explains the meaning of the negation of faith from them in His saying "you have not believed": it is not the absence of any affirmation by the tongue, but the absence of its firm establishment and the binding of the heart upon it, since there remained among them some remnant of doubt, as its being placed opposite to His saying ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, then they did not doubt﴾ [al-Hujurat: 15] indicates.

The verb "entered" in His saying ﴿faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ is used metaphorically for firm establishment and lack of wavering, because one who enters a place settles and remains in it, while one who leaves it is quick to depart from it, ready to turn away.

This "lamma" is a sister of "lam", and it indicates that the negation expressed by it is connected to the time of speaking; that is the distinction between it and "lam", its sister. This indication of the continuation of the negation up to the time of the speaker usually signals that what is negated by it is expected to occur. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: what is in "lamma" of the sense of expectation indicates that these people have believed afterwards.

This is an implication of the constructions, and it is one of the subtleties of Arabic. Abu Hayyan disagreed about it, but al-Zamakhshari is an authority in taste, whom Abu Hayyan does not approach; for this reason His saying ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ is not a repetition of His saying "you have not believed".

His saying ﴿And if you obey Allah and His Messenger, He will not deprive you [the reward] of your deeds at all﴾ is a guidance to the remedy of the state of sickness in their hearts from the weakness of faith: that if they obey Allah and His Messenger, their faith will be obtained, for among what Allah commanded through His Messenger (ﷺ) is the explanation of the articles of faith, by turning to learn from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during their stay in Madina, instead of occupying themselves with reproach and insinuation in seeking charities.

The meaning of "lā yaliturkum" is "will not diminish you": it is said "lātahu" like "bā'ahu" (he sold it). This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and Banu Asad. It is also said "altahu altan" like "amarahu" (he ordered him), and this is the dialect of Ghatafan. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And We did not diminish them from their deeds anything﴾ [al-Tur: 21] in Surat al-Tur.

The first form was read by the majority of reciters, and the second by Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub. For Abu 'Amr there are two transmissions concerning the realisation of the hamza in it and its softening to an alif: al-Duri transmitted from him the realisation of the hamza, and al-Susi transmitted from him its softening.

The pronoun of the nominative in "yaliturkum" refers to the name of Allah, and He did not say "lā yalitākumā" with the dual pronoun, because Allah alone is the one who bestows the recompense, not the Messenger (ﷺ).

The meaning: if you sincerely establish faith as Allah and His Messenger have commanded you, Allah will accept your deeds which you mentioned, namely that you came obedient to Islam without fighting.

His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) of teaching them that Allah overlooks their lie if they repent, and an encouragement to make their faith sincere, because the Forgiving is abundant and intense in forgiveness, and from the excess of His forgiveness is that He rewards the righteous deeds done in a state of disbelief without counting them, so that when their doer believes he is rewarded for his faith alone; and that is from the excess of His mercy toward His servants.

The ordering of "Merciful" after "Forgiving" is because mercy is the root of forgiveness, and it is the nature of the cause to be mentioned after what it explains.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verse 15:

[Page 267]
﴿Indeed, the believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger and then have not doubted and have striven with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. Those are the truthful.﴾

This is an explanation (ta'lil) of His saying, "You have not believed" up to His saying, "in your hearts." It is among what the Messenger ﷺ was commanded to say to the Bedouins, meaning: the believers are none other than those who have believed and whose faith has not been mixed with doubt (irtiyab) or skepticism (tashakkuk).

The particle (innama) is for restriction (hasr), and (inna), which is part of it, is also for causation (ta'lil) and stands in the place of the resultative fa' (fa' al-tafri'), meaning: you have not been believers only because faith is contradicted by doubt.

The restriction is relative (idafi), meaning: the believers who possess these attributes are other than these Bedouins.

Thus it conveys that these Bedouins lack faith because the whole set of these attributes is absent from them.

Since the restriction is relative, its purpose is only to affirm the attribute for other than the one restricted, in order to exclude those spoken of from being believers. It does not necessitate that the reality of faith is not constituted except by the entire set of these attributes, because counting striving in the cause of Allah alongside the two attributes of faith and the absence of doubt about it prevents that, since one who holds back from jihad does not lose the description of faith, as a Muslim does not become a disbeliever by committing major sins according to the People of the Truth. Anything other than this is a manifest error, for otherwise the community of Islam as a whole would be annulled, except for a small group and for brief periods.

The purpose of incorporating the mention of jihad is to honor the merit of the believing mujahidun and to encourage those who have entered faith to prepare for jihad, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say to the Bedouins who were left behind: "You will be called to a people of great military might; you will fight them, or they will submit."﴾ [al-Fath: 16], and so on.

The (thumma) in His saying ﴿then have not doubted﴾ is for successive ranking (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), as is its usage in conjoining sentences. Thus in (thumma) there is an indication that the absence of doubt about their faith is of higher rank than faith itself, since upon it the standing of faith depends,

[Page 268]
and this is an allusion to the explanation of His saying: ﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14], meaning: because of what doubt stirs within you concerning some of what you have professed, of what Allah has knowledge of.

His saying ﴿Those are the truthful﴾ is a restriction, and it is also a relative restriction, meaning: they are the truthful, not you in your saying "We have believed."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verse 16:

﴿Say: "Do you inform Allah of your religion? And Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth, and Allah is Knowing of all things."﴾

The verb "qul" (say) is repeated to indicate that those addressed by this speech are the Bedouins to whom he was commanded to say: "You have not believed" and so on. It was repeated because the separation between the two statements by the succession of sentences had become long. So this is connected to His saying ﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14] in the manner of an explanation connected to what it explains. For this reason the interrogative sentence is not conjoined by a conjunction.

The sentence "qul" is parenthetical (mu'taridah) between the explaining sentence and the explained sentence.

It was said: when they heard His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: You have not believed﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14], and the verse, they came to the Prophet ﷺ and swore that they were believers, so His saying was revealed: ﴿Say: Do you inform Allah of your religion?﴾. This was not narrated through a known chain of transmission; rather al-Baghawi mentioned it as tafsir. Had it been so, Allah would have rebuked them for the false oaths, just as He rebuked the hypocrites in the surah of (Bara'ah) with His saying: ﴿They will swear by Allah, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you," destroying themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 42], and the verse. I have not found that through an accepted chain, so this verse is among what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was commanded to say to them.

Ta'lim (teaching, informing) is an intensification of conveying knowledge to the one taught, because the form of the verb with the doubled middle radical (tafil) implies strength in the occurrence of the action, as in tafriq (separating) and tafsir (explaining). It is said: a'lamahu and 'allamahu, just as it is said: anba'ahu and nabba'ahu. This indicates that they exerted themselves and strained in seeking evidence of the sincerity of their faith in order to persuade the Messenger ﷺ with it. He had informed them that Allah negated from them the firmness of faith, so their attempt to persuade him points to an attempt to persuade Allah with what He knows to be otherwise.

The letter "ba'" in "bi-dinikum" is extra (za'idah), for emphasizing the attachment of the verb to its object, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And wipe your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], and the saying of al-Nabighah:

*Page 269*

*To you are the two goods; the earth has concealed you, one alone...*

The interrogative in ﴿Do you inform Allah of your religion?﴾ is used for reproach, and the reproach has been reinforced by the circumstantial clause in His saying: ﴿And Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾.
In this there is a rebuke for their ignorance, since they tried to conceal their inner state from the One who has knowledge of everything.

The sentence ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ is a concluding generalization (tadhyil), because "all things" is more general than ﴿what is in the heavens and what is on the earth﴾, for Allah knows His own attributes and knows the existents that are higher than the heavens, such as the Throne.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 49, verse 17:

﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have submitted (to Islam). Say: "Do not consider your submission a favour to me. Rather, Allah bestows a favour upon you that He has guided you to faith, if you are truthful."﴾

This is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i), intended to nullify what the Banu Asad displayed before the Prophet ﷺ as a distinction of theirs, namely that they embraced Islam without being compelled by a military expedition.

Al-mann (favour-reckoning) is mentioning a blessing and a kindness so that the one who receives it acknowledges it to the one who did it. It may be explicit, like the words of Sabra ibn 'Amr al-Faqa'si:

أتَنْسى دِفاعِي عَنْكَ إذْ أنْتَ مُسْلَمٌ وقَدْ سالَ مِن ذُلٍّ عَلَيْكَ قَراقِرُ

It may also be by allusion (ta'rid), where the benefactor mentions some of his dealings with the one he favours, which are in fact beneficial to that person, with an indication that he did not intend mere reporting. Like the words of al-Ra'i addressing 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan:

فَآزَرَتُ آلَ أبِي خُبَيْبٍ وافِدًايَوْمًا أُرِيدَ لِبَيْعَتِي تَبْدِيلا

Abu Khubayb: the kunya of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr.

The statement of the Banu Asad included both types of mann, for they said: "We did not fight you as Muhārib, Ghatafan and Hawazin fought you," and they said: "We have come to you with our burdens and our families."

"An aslamu" is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, which is the ba' of transitivity; it is said: "manna 'alayhi bi-kadha" (he bestowed upon him such-and-such). Likewise His saying "la tamunnu 'alayya islamakum." However, the first is regular with (an) and (an), while the second is transmitted (sama'i), and it is common.

They said to the Prophet ﷺ: "We have believed (amanna)," as Allah related just before. Here He named it "islam" in accordance with His saying: ﴿But say: "We have submitted (aslamna)"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14], meaning that what they reckoned as a favour upon you is submission (islam), not faith (iman).

By the particle (bal) it is established that what they reckoned as a favour, if it was genuine submission agreeing with faith, then the favour belongs to Allah, because He guided them to it, so they submitted willingly.

He named it "iman" just now in accommodation to their claim, because the context is one of the favour being Allah's; so the fitting approach is to go along with their claim that they had believed: that is, even if it is supposed that you believed as you claim, your faith is a blessing with which Allah has favoured you.

For this reason He followed it with His saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾. He first negated that what they reckon as a favour is true, then He further indicated that the superiority in what they claimed for themselves, were they truthful, is rather the bounty of Allah.

The word islam has been attributed to their pronoun because they brought what is called islam, as in His saying ﴿But say: "We have submitted"﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14].

Iman is mentioned in the definite form with the article of nature (lam al-jins), because it is a reality in itself, and they are those who are associated with it.

The present tense is used in "yamunnuna" although their reckoning occurred in the past, to bring to mind the state of their reckoning, how they reckon with what they have not done. It is like the present tense in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieve mock those who believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 212], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The present tense is used in His saying: ﴿Rather Allah bestows a favour upon you﴾ because it is a favour that is supposed (mafrud), since what is favoured with has not yet occurred.

In it there is an indication that He will bestow upon them the faith, as in His saying: ﴿and faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ [al-Hujurat: 14]. This is among the wonderful variations of speech, so that the listener is placed, with each of its kinds, in its proper settlement; and those who are perceptive of these subtleties are like them.

The placing of the subject (musnad ilayhi) before the verbal predicate (musnad fi'li) is for the purpose of emphasis (taqwiya), like: "huwa yu'tt al-jazil" (he gives abundantly), as 'Abd al-Qahir gave as an example.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 49, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

This concluding statement (*tadhyil*) was appended to their upright conduct in truth so that they would know that Allah does not conceal, and that He does not lie, because He knows every hidden thing in the heavens and the earth. In the Jahiliyyah, the fundamental attributes of God did not occur to many of them.

Some of them may have known them, such as Zuhayr in his saying:

*So do not conceal from Allah what is in your souls, that it may be hidden; whatever you conceal, Allah knows it.*

(Perhaps this is among the effects of his Christianity.)

The affirmation of the statement with *inna* (indeed) is because they were in the condition of one who denies that Allah knows the unseen. They lied against the Prophet ﷺ even though they knew that he was sent by Allah, so their lying against him was like lying against Allah.

This sentence affirms the content of the two sentences before it: ﴿And Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾ [al-Hujurat: 16] and ﴿And Allah is, of all things, Knowing﴾ [al-Hujurat: 16]. However, this one adds the explicit statement that He knows the unseen matters, lest someone imagine that the generality in the two preceding sentences is a customary generality, analogous to human knowledge.

The sentence ﴿and Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ is coordinated (*ma'tuf*) upon the sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah knows the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, in the manner of *'atf al-akhass 'ala al-a'amm* (coordination of the more specific upon the more general). Because He mentioned that He knows the unseen, and it is the nature of the unseen that it is not seen, He coordinated upon it His knowledge of the perceptible things, as a precaution lest they imagine that Allah knows the hidden recesses of souls and what passes through thoughts, but does not know the observable things. This is similar to the saying of many philosophers: the Creator knows universals but does not know particulars. For this reason, the attribute "Seeing" (*basir*) was chosen here.

The majority of reciters read ﴿bima ta'malun﴾ with the *ta'* of address. Ibn Kathir read it with the *ya'* of the third person.

Surah Qaf

It was named in the age of the Companions "Surat Qaf," pronounced with the letters: *qaf*, *bi-qaf*, *alif*, *fa'*.

Muslim narrated from Qutbah ibn Malik that the Prophet ﷺ recited in the Dawn prayer Surah ﴿Qaf, by the Glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1]. He may have said "Qaf," meaning in the first rak'ah.

Muslim also narrated from Umm Hisham bint Harithah ibn al-Nu'man: "I took ﴿Qaf, by the Glorious Qur'an﴾ only from the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; he recited it every day on the pulpit when he addressed the people."

Muslim narrated from Jabir ibn Samurah that the Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the Fajr (dawn) prayer with *Qaf* ﴿and the Glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1]. Thus the orthography (*rasm*) of *Qaf* is three letters. His saying "in the Fajr" means the Dawn prayer, because it is the one he prayed in the mosque in congregation; as for the voluntary Dawn prayer, he used to pray it in his house.

In the Muwatta' and Muslim, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked Abu Waqid al-Laythi: "What did the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recite in al-Adha and al-Fitr?" He said: "He recited in them *Qaf*." Thus the orthography of *Qaf* is three letters, like the narration of Jabir ibn Samurah, ﴿and the Glorious Qur'an﴾ [Qaf: 1] and ﴿The Hour has come near, and the moon has split﴾ [al-Qamar: 1].

It is among the surahs named after the letters occurring at their beginnings, like Ta-Ha, Sad, Qaf, and Ya-Sin, because each surah is distinguished by the number of letters occurring at its beginning, such that when it is called by them it is not confused with another surah.

In al-Itqan it is said that it is called Surat al-Basiqat, with the definite article, and he did not attribute it to anyone. The likely view is that this naming is on the basis of an adjective for an omitted noun, meaning "the Surah of the tall palm trees (*al-Naxl al-Basiqat*)," referring to His saying: ﴿And the tall palm trees with layered spathes﴾ [Qaf: 10].

This surah is entirely Meccan. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: by consensus of the exegetes.

In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi and in al-Itqan, from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak, there is an exception of one verse: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf: 38], which they said was revealed concerning the Jews, meaning in refutation of them when they said that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six days, then rested on the seventh day, which is Saturday. That is, the saying of the Jews was heard in Medina, meaning that it was attached to this surah due to the appropriateness of its placement.

Although this meaning is a subtle one in the verse, it does not necessitate that the verse was revealed in Medina, for Allah knew that and revealed it to His Messenger ﷺ. Moreover, some opinions of the Jews were among things that the people of Mecca discussed before Islam, receiving them as stories and reports. After the mission, they used to ask the Jews about the matter of prophethood and the prophets. Furthermore, Allah's will to nullify the delusions of the Jews does not require delaying their nullification until they were heard; rather, something that nullifies them may come before they spread among people, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure, while the earth entirely will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded in His right hand﴾ [al-Zumar: 67], for it was revealed in Mecca.

It is reported that a rabbi of the Jews came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "Indeed, Allah places the heavens on one finger, the earths on one finger, the seas on one finger, and the mountains on one finger, then He says: 'I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?'" The Prophet ﷺ then recited the verse. What is intended by its recitation is His saying: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [al-An'am: 91], and an allusion to the misunderstanding of the Jews regarding the attributes of Allah.

It is the thirty-fourth surah in the order of revelation according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Mursalat and before Surat La Uqsimu bihadha al-Balad.

The enumerators have unanimously counted its verses as forty-five.

* * *

The purposes of this surah:

The first: the exaltation of the status of the Qur'an.

The second: that they denied the Messenger ﷺ because he is a human being.

The third: the argument for establishing the Resurrection, and that it is not greater than the initial creation of the heavens and what is in them, and the creation of the earth and what is on it, and the growth of plants and fruits from the water of the sky, and that this is a parable for resurrection after death.

The fourth: comparing the polytheists in their denial of the message and the Resurrection to some past nations known to them, and the threat that what befell those would befall them.

The fifth: the threat of punishment of the Hereafter beginning from the moment of one's death agony, and the mention of the terror of the Day of Reckoning.

The sixth: the promise to the believers of the bliss of the Hereafter.

The seventh: consoling the Prophet ﷺ regarding their denial of him, and commanding him to devote himself to the obedience of his Lord and to defer the matter of those who deny until the Day of Resurrection, and that if Allah willed, He would seize them now, but the wisdom of Allah required their deferment; and that the Prophet ﷺ was not charged with compelling them to Islam, but was only commanded to remind them with the Qur'an.

The eighth: praise of the believers in the Resurrection, that they are the ones who remember by the Qur'an.

The ninth: the comprehensiveness of Allah's knowledge of hidden things and the thoughts of souls.
